📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tyson Fury is detailing a decadelong personal battle.

The boxing champ shared in his upcoming Netflix documentary that he was diagnosed with schizophrenia back in 2015, the same year he became the heavyweight champion of the world following his victory over Wladimir Klitschko.

“Words can’t explain the darkness I was in,” Tyson says in the self-titled doc, out Nov. 27, according to Deadline. “I came from the living version of the pits of hellfire. And I 100 percent thought at times I’d end up in a padded room with the door locked, and that scared me so much.”.

Two years later, he got even more insight into the war raging inside his mind.

“I was waking up in the night like this, the anxiety was crippling me. I just could not overcome it,” he explains. “Completely gone, and that’s when I went and saw the psychiatrist down in London. She asked me like a gazillion questions, and I ticked all the boxes, whatever was going on. Depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder.”.

And while the 38-year-old only just began addressing his mental health struggles in recent years, his father John Fury shares in the doc that he saw signs of the athlete’s diagnoses all along.

“I can tell you this: When I look back, it’s always been there,” the patriarch admits. “Me being who I am and no understanding of anything, I didn’t want to see a depressed kid—and if I did see it, I paid no mind to it.”.

That’s because if he did, he’d have to face his own mental health struggles. “But I understand now,” John adds. “It’s an illness, a terrible illness. I suffer with it myself.”.

But on Halloween 2017, Tyson—who shares seven kids with wife Paris Fury—decided he would make a change.

It has been revealed that “I went out and I was embarrassed of how I looked,” he recalls. “I had this major costume on, a glow in the dark skeleton suit and I thought no one would recognize me in this.”.

But instead of focusing on keeping a low profile, he couldn’t help but take a hard look at his life.

Sources indicate that “I looked around me and I could see all like young people and I thought I’ve had the world in my hands and I threw it all away,” he notes. “And now, I’m just a fat mess, addicted to alcohol and, go home.”.

But it was hitting rock bottom that allowed him to eventually reach the pinnacle of his life.

“I just noted, ‘I can’t do this on my own anymore. I need your help,’” he indicates in the doc. “And that was the part, the comeback.”.

Tyson Fury debuts on Netflix Nov. 27.

Keep reading for more stars who have spoken out about their mental health struggles….

The Grammy winner has been very open about how she protects her energy, such as ignoring haters on social media, while also sharing her advice for those who may need help.

According to recent reports, "When people ask me what I'd say to somebody looking for advice on mental health, the only thing I can say is patience," she told Vogue. "I had patience with myself. I didn't take that last step. I waited. Things fade.".

She has advocated for finding the methods that help you best, which for her, according to Health, can include medication, listing ten positive things in her life for every negative thought and getting plenty of exercise.

"Sometimes I don't know what's worse trying to avoid the virus or the waves of depression that come with this latest norm," she shared on Twitter. Katy talked about how she manages those waves, writing, "There is not really anywhere to go besides my car. So I go to my car a lot. That is my safe space.".

The model, who teamed up with designer Kenneth Cole to raise awareness for The Mental Health Coalition, spoke on Good Morning America about her own experiences with anxiety.

She recalled after her panic attacks started recurring, she, "finally kind of got the information that I needed about it.".

"For me, I have good days and I have some really anxious days, so I'm really off and on," Kendall expressed, adding that was why she wanted to become involved with the movement. "What I hope to accomplish is for people to not feel as alone.".

The rapper (real name Radric Davis) revealed in his October 2025 book Episodes: The Diary of a Recovering Mad Man that he had been diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, which prompted a mental health episode in 2020.

Sources indicate that “After that, I was like, ‘Man, I got to really just hold myself accountable and take care of my health,’” he said on an episode of The Breakfast Club. “I don’t never want to have an episode again. I’m gonna see a therapist, [even] if I have to take medicine.”.

In addition to his hope that his vulnerability would help others in need, Gucci Mane stated that his kids Ice Davis and Iceland Ka’oir Davis with wife Keyshia Ka’Oir inspired him to seek help amid his episode.

In a recent development, “My wife was pregnant with my little boy,” he continued. “I don’t want to raise a family and then my mental health [is] gone. What if I have an episode I can’t come back from? So, I just started doing the work and started seeking help.”.

In October 2026, the daughter of Teresa Giudice and Joe Giudice shared she was getting treatment for bipolar disorder in a candid enhancement about her mental health journey.

Industry observers note that "I do struggle with mental health issues," Milania told followers in an Oct. 12 Instagram video. "I am bipolar. I struggle with depression, anxiety, PTSD and ADHD and I am not ashamed of any of my mental health disorders because I'm currently at a treatment center, my mom's on her way to come visit me today.".

The then-20-year-old added that "this summer hit me like a bus" after Milania was arrested for assault in May and her best friend Victoria Zardoya died suddenly in July.

According to recent reports, "A lot of things happened in a short amount of time and I'm trying to just process everything," the University of Tampa student noted. "It's really hard being in the public light while you go through things in life.".

The Gossip Girl alum detailed his experience as a child actor with what he described as "body dysmorphia.".

“I know that I hated my body,” Penn told The Guardian in April 2025, “and simply wanted a different one.”.

In response to the weight he gained following his parents' divorce, he added,  “There was just a period where, coming out of depression and isolation, I was jumping wilfully into, but also being thrust into, this world where the more conventionally beautiful I seemed, the more successful I might be, the more value I might have.”.

Despite the mental struggles, though, Penn credited his ability to persist to his spirituality.

“That is what allowed me to persevere through the disillusionment, all the things I’d been grappling with,” he explained, “and then come back to it all, but with hopefully some kind of inner transformation.”.

The Scrubs alum has been vocal about her past difficult relationship with food.

“Some may call it an eating disorder, I just call it my life,” she noted on the The Funny Thing Is podcast. “My drug of choice was always food. I did crazy s--t with it.”.

She added, “I would over-exercise, and there was a sprinkle of bulimia in there.”.

Though she has confessed her struggles with her diet, she has also shared her progress with her health and fitness goals.

“When I was 23, I cut all sugar out of my diet, quit drinking, and found yoga and breathing and stretching,” she told Bon Appétit in 2017. “That’s the best Ritalin you could give anyone.".

According to recent reports, she continued, "I’m an actress with food issues and body image issues—that's real. But I'm trying to heal that part of myself and also handle my physical issues naturally by putting the best things into my body.".

The Full House alum reflected on her mental health journey and navigating her battle with depression.

"It's very difficult to speak out about it, even to your most trusted people," she shared on her Candace Cameron Bure Podcast. "At least for me, I feel like I should be strong enough to overcome that and then it feels so weak.".

The Black Adam actor has been open about having depression and how it can be difficult for men to talk about their mental health.

"We all go thru the sludge/shit and depression never discriminates. Took me a long time to realize it but the key is to not be afraid to open up," he wrote on Twitter. "Especially us dudes have a tendency to keep it in. You're not alone.".

The Duke of Sussex helped break down some of the stigma around seeking help for mental health when, in an interview with the Telegraph, he opened up about his own journey with therapy. As he told the outlet, "The experience I have had is that once you start talking about it, you realize that actually you're part of quite a big club.".

Another proponent of seeking professional help, the Empire star has been open about her struggles with depression."I have a therapist that I speak to," she previously told Variety. "That's the only way I can get through it.".

Taraji even started The Boris Lawrence Henson Foundation, which works to reduce the stigma around mental health in the African American community and also works to increase the number of Black therapists.

The Grammy winner explained that experiences with an eating disorder and stage freight led her to start a form of PTSD treatment called MDMA and and psilocybin therapy.

“I was touring without stage fright for the first time,” she told Rolling Stone in May 2025. “There was a hook around my guts and everyone in the room was having the same feeling, [like] there’d been a huge pressure change. It made me realize how much I love and kind of need that very deep, visceral response to feel my music.”.

She added that her renewed focus on her mental health, as well as her decision to stop taking birth control, caused her understanding of her own gender to become “more expansive.”.

“I felt like stopping taking my birth control, I had cut some sort of cord between myself and this regulated femininity,” she continued. “It sounds crazy, but I felt that all of a sudden, I was off the map of femininity. And I totally believed that that allowed things to open up.”.

According to recent reports, "When I was in middle school, I was struggling with severe anxiety and depression and the help and support I received from my family and a therapist saved my life," the Riverdale actress wrote on Instagram in 2017. "Asking for help is the first step. You are more precious to this world than you'll ever know.".

The “What He Didn’t Do” singer shared insight into what her life has been like during her yearslong battle with anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

It has been revealed that “I would have told you three years ago my anxiety started during my divorce in Covid,” Carly said an August 2025 episode of Bunnie Xo’s Dumb Blonde podcast. “But I’ve had crippling OCD since I was a child.”.

In a recent development, “I got really conditioned over the last 10 years to just zip it up and deal with it, and it just kind of got to a place where a couple years ago I just had to really start back into therapy, start really, like, trying to figure out all of these different things,” she continued. “Like, recognizing OCD was something—no, that didn’t come in 2020, that’s been there since I was 6 or 7.”.

While the cookbook author is the proud parent to four kiddos, she's also been open about postpartum depression that many latest mothers experience but feel like they cannot talk about.

Sources indicate that "It got easier and easier to say it aloud every time," she wrote in an open letter to Glamour in 2017. "I want people to know it can happen to anybody and I don't want people who have it to feel embarrassed or to feel alone.".

While promoting her book Mirror, Mirror, the model opened up to The Edit magazine about facing depression and suicidal thoughts as a teenager, saying she felt "something dark" in her during that time.

"I relied too much on love, too much on other people to make me happy, and I needed to learn to be happy by myself," Cara told the publication, via W. "So now I can be by myself, I can be happy. It took me a long time.".

The "Thank U, Next" artist has encouraged fans to seek help if they need, responding to a Twitter user who joked about wondering who Ariana's therapist is with, "lmaoaoo this is funny as f--k but in all honesty therapy has saved my life so many times.".

It has been revealed that "If you're afraid to ask for help, don't be," she continued. "u don't have to be in constant pain & u can process trauma. I've got a lot of work to do but it's a start to even be aware that it's possible.".

The singer has been open about her journey with addiction, sobriety, mental health and more, including many of those aspects of her life within her music.

She also continually reminds fans that working on your mental health is an ongoing process where there will be some bad days, previously writing on Instagram, "A reminder to anyone struggling out there - this life is a journey with tons of ups and downs but you can't give up.".

Not only has the actress taken on roles that deal with mental health, such as her role as Rue in the teen drama Euphoria, she's also addressed those issues in her own life, too.

Back in 2013, Zendaya wrote on her now-defunct app that she struggled with anxiety after an appearance on Ellen where her mic went out. She has since learned ways to manage those feelings, adding, "Sometimes you just have to take a step back so things stop stressin' you.".

The singer candidly described her mental health journey with WSJ Magazine, saying, "My highs were really high, and my lows would take me out for weeks at a time.".

In a recent development, "I found out I do suffer from mental health complications," she shared. "I got on the right medication, and my life has been completely changed.".

The Grammy winner made it her mission to spread kindness and be open about mental health, including her own.

Industry observers note that "I have struggled for a long time, both being public and not public about my mental health issues or my mental illness," she remarked during the Global Changemakers Award at Children Mending Hearts' Empathy Rocks fundraiser in 2018. "But, I truly believe that secrets keep you sick.".

Novo states Wegovy injection lowers BMI and obesity rates in children in trial

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Novo on Monday released full results from a late-stage trial showing its blockbuster Wegovy injection helped children ages 6 to under 12 with obesity shed weight, significantly lowering their body mass index.
  • In a recent development, wegovy reduced BMI by an estimated 19.7 percentage points on average compared with a placebo at 68 weeks, with BMI falling 17.4% among children receiving the drug and rising 2.2% among those receiving a placebo.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Novo on Monday released full results from a late-stage trial showing its blockbuster Wegovy injection helped children ages 6 to under 12 with obesity shed weight, significantly lowering their body mass index.

In a recent development, wegovy reduced BMI by an estimated 19.7 percentage points on average compared with a placebo at 68 weeks, with BMI falling 17.4% among children receiving the drug and rising 2.2% among those receiving a placebo. Those results assumed patients stayed on treatment during the trial.

Recent findings suggest that when evaluating all children in the study, including those who discontinued treatment, Wegovy lowered BMI by an estimated average of 16.2 percentage points more than the placebo at 68 weeks. All 167 kids in the study received lifestyle modifications throughout the trial, including a ​reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.

It has been revealed that the detailed results mark an encouraging step forward in treating childhood obesity — a chronic disease that can carry serious cardiovascular, metabolic and psychosocial consequences but has had few treatment options for younger children. When left unaddressed, childhood obesity can extend into adulthood, bringing earlier and more severe health complications.

"This is a very significant disease burden in this very young patient population," remarked Dr. Andrea Traina, Novo's medical director lead of obesity.

Industry observers note that in 2025, the disease affected an estimated roughly 177 million children and teens ages 5 to 19 worldwide, according to the World Obesity Federation. That figure is projected to rise to 228 million by 2040.

In a recent development, while Wegovy is already approved to treat obesity in children ages 12 and older, there are currently no approved medications for those under 12. The latest results offer evidence that Wegovy can potentially fill that treatment gap, safely and effectively reducing the severity of the disease in children as young as 6.

Industry observers note that in Novo's trial, 85% of children started with moderate to severe obesity, which corresponds to BMI thresholds of 35 and above and 40 or higher, respectively. Nearly half already had at least one obesity-related complication, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol or sleep apnea.

But more than 40% of children treated with Wegovy were no longer classified as having obesity after 68 weeks of the trial, assuming patients stayed on treatment. Novo initially shared that result in September.

"We are driving towards control of this chronic disease in that patient population when they are still so young and at such high risk for more advanced and accelerated disease progression because they developed it so early," Traina said.

Novo said Wegovy's overall safety and tolerability among children — how well patients managed the drug — were consistent with those seen in ​trials ⁠with adults. The firm added that it observed no safety concerns related to growth or pubertal development in the kids.

Still, the two-year study does not establish whether treating obesity earlier can change its long-term trajectory, or what treatment and maintenance might look like as children grow into adulthood, Traina remarked.

"That is something that is still an evidence gap," she stated, pointing to the potential of future research.

The Himalayas tower below the clouds, capped in icy snow in fresh snapshots captured from aboard the International Space Station.

Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk was looking out one of the windows aboard the space station when the most incredible view came into focus  — and thankfully he had a camera handy and was able to capture these striking scenes of the Himalayas from space.

Above the mountain range, fluffy clouds hang in the atmosphere. Below, the expansive Himalayas are covered in bright snow and ice, which looks somehow both white and blue at the same time as the bright sunlight streaks across the breathtaking expanse.

This frosty winter scene showcases the mountain range from orbit, from about 250 miles (400 kilometers) above Earth's surface. But even from this distance, the magnitude of this mountain range is palpable. The Himalayas stretch across five different countries including Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan. And the Himalayas include some of the highest mountain peaks on planet Earth, including Mount Everest.

Himalayas 🗻 https://t.co/IzGzu20H4QNovember 17, 2026.

According to recent reports, from orbit around Earth, you might expect even the largest landmarks on our planet to appear miniscule. But somehow, in these photographs snapped by Kutryk during NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission, even from hundreds of miles above our planet you can really see and feel the immense scale of this mammoth mountain range.

It's unclear exactly where above the mountain range these photographs were taken, but it is always amazing to think that within these sweeping landscapes are people living their lives, likely unaware that an astronaut is taking in the beauty of their home.

In a recent development, perhaps somewhere hidden under the clouds in one of Kutryk's photographs are hikers climbing up the side of Mt. Everest, completing their own bucket list adventure as the astronauts watching from above complete theirs.

Kwame Brathwaite, photographer of 'Black is Beautiful' movement, dies at 85

📅 04 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 4 min read (761 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.
  • Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.
  • His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, unveiled his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.

Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.

His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, unveiled his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”.

Brathwaite’s work has been the subject of resurgent interest from curators, historians and collectors in recent years, and his first major institutional retrospective, which was organized by the Aperture Foundation, made its debut in 2019 at the Skirball Cultural Center in Los Angeles before touring the country.

According to recent reports, brathwaite was born in 1938 to Barbadian immigrants, in what he referred to as “the People’s Republic of Brooklyn” in Latest York, though his family moved from there to Harlem and then to the South Bronx when Brathwaite was 5 years old. He attended the School of Industrial Art (now the High School of Art and Design) and, according to profiles of Brathwaite in T Magazine and Vice, was drawn to photography by two moments. The first was in August of 1955, when a 17-year-old Brathwaite encountered David Jackson’s haunting photograph of a brutalized Emmett Till in his open casket. The second was in 1956, when — after he and his brother Elombe co-founded the African Jazz Arts Society and Studios (AJASS) — Brathwaite saw a young man taking photos in a dark jazz club without the use of a flash, and his mind became alight with possibility.

Using a Hasselblad medium-format camera, Brathwaite attempted to do the same, learning to work with limited light in a manner that enhanced the visual narrative of his imagery. He would soon also develop a darkroom technique that enriched and deepened how Black skin would appear in his photography, honing the practice in a small darkroom in his Harlem apartment. Brathwaite went on to photograph jazz legends performing throughout the 1950s and ’60s, including Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Thelonious Monk and others.

“You want to get the feeling, the mood that you’re experiencing when they’re playing,” Brathwaite told Aperture Magazine in 2017. “That’s the thing. You want to capture that.”.

A 106-year-old from the Philippines is Vogue's oldest ever cover model.

By the early 1960s, alongside the rest of AJASS, Brathwaite began using his photography and organizing prowess to consciously push back against whitewashed, Eurocentric beauty standards. The group came up with the concept of the Grandassa Models, young Black women whom Brathwaite would photograph, celebrating and accentuating their features. In 1962, AJASS organized “Naturally ’62”, a fashion show held in a Harlem club called the Purple Manor and featuring the models. The show would go on to be held regularly until 1992. In 1966, Brathwaite married his wife Sikolo, a Grandassa Model whom he had met on the street the year prior when he asked if he could take her portrait. The two remained married for the rest of Brathwaite’s life.

By the 1970s, Brathwaite’s focus on jazz shifted to other forms of popular Black music. In 1974, he traveled to Africa with the Jackson Five to document their tour, also photographing the historic “Rumble in the Jungle” boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman in what’s now the Democratic Republic of Congo that same year. Commissions in this era also saw Brathwaite photographing Nina Simone, Stevie Wonder, Sly and the Family Stone, Bob Marley and other music legends.

Creating for community: The Black designers placing identity and heritage at the center of their brands.

Throughout the ensuing decades, Brathwaite continued to explore and develop his mode of photography, all through the lens of the “Black is Beautiful” ethos. In 2016, Brathwaite joined the roster of Philip Martin Gallery in Los Angeles, and he was continuing to photograph commissions as recently as 2018, when he shot artist and stylist Joanne Petit-Frère for The Newly introduced Yorker.

T Magazine’s 2021 profile, published on the occasion of Brathwaite’s retrospective traveling to the Blanton Museum of Art in Austin, Texas, noted that the photographer’s health was failing such that he was unable to be interviewed for the article. A separate exhibition, “Kwame Brathwaite: Things Well Worth Waiting For,” is presently on view at the Art Institute of Chicago, where it will remain until July 24.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ngumoha stars as Liverpool thrash 10-man Man Utd.

"Sacked in the morning, you're getting sacked in the morning...".

Fourteen minutes in, arms folded, two goals down at Liverpool and with his Manchester United team reduced to 10 men, Mauricio Pochettino could not ignore the cruel taunts echoing around Anfield.

What on earth must Pochettino have been thinking as he stood at the edge of his technical area?

In distance terms, he was 3,800 miles from his last managerial assignment against Haiti in Cincinnati in the early hours of Wednesday morning UK time.

In difficulty levels, it must have felt significantly further than that.

By the final whistle, as Liverpool's gleeful supporters alternated between singing about the notion of Pochettino's immediate dismissal, United "going down" and celebrating "Poch is at the wheel", the Argentine head coach would have been starting to understand the scale of the task he has taken on by quitting his United States job.

He had just watched United be dismantled 4-0 by their oldest rivals, with Leny Yoro's eighth-minute red card and two quickfire goals soon after representing just about the worst possible start imaginable to his reign as manager.

His team sit 19th in the 20-team Premier League after 11 games, already 20 points behind leaders Arsenal.

"Animals of the grass, we like to smell it and feel it," was the memorable phrase Pochettino came out with during Friday's pre-match media conference, explaining how he has missed the day-to-day nature of club football.

Listen to former United skipper Roy Keane's post-match summary of the loss on Sky Sports and a very different smell comes to mind.

For the record, it was the joint-worst result for any fresh United boss, matching the 4-0 loss Lal Hilditch suffered against Bolton in October 1926.

Hilditch lasted 30 games and never managed another team.

Pochettino endures nightmare start as Man Utd lose to Liverpool.

The red card that changed Liverpool-Man Utd: correct call?

Yoro sees red as Ngumoha shines - Liverpool v Man Utd player ratings.

Liverpool run riot for Pochettinoâs nightmare debut.

Keane is not one for holding back, so his response to his old side's latest setback was predictable.

Sources indicate that "Fans are applauding the players [at the end]. Applauding what? Applauding rubbish," he said. "When do the players take responsibility for some of the decision-making?".

There were enough images of chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox broadcast during the game by Sky Sports to suggest there is a wider debate to be had about the quality of the players at Pochettino's disposal.

On Friday, Berrada stated this season's squad was "fundamentally better" than the one which finished third last season. Few would agree with that, and presumably Keane is among the group who would challenge Berrada's assertion.

Pochettino, 54, shed tears of emotion when he explained his difficulty in deciding to quit the United States job and take up an opportunity at a club he has flirted with for the best part of a decade but, only now, has been given the chance to coach.

It was easy to imagine him being reduced to tears again as Sunday's debacle unfolded, a nightmare afternoon in Liverpool coming at the end of a chaotic week of travel.

He arrived to begin his new role as United head coach on Wednesday after agreeing a two-and-a-half-year contract.

Recent findings suggest that the USA beat Haiti 2-0 in Cincinnati in his final game in charge on Tuesday, with Pochettino flying directly to Manchester on a private jet after the game. He landed at about 11:30 GMT before heading to the club's Carrington training ground - and his feet have barely touched the floor since.

Mauricio Pochettino gives his post-match verdict on Liverpool v Man Utd.

Pochettino was bullish when speaking to the media after this 4-0 defeat.

Although he began his first answer by saying he went to referee Sam Barrott after the final whistle to "present his respect", he became increasingly more forceful in his view Leny Yoro should not have been sent off.

After dismissing the sorry statistic that United have conceded 19 goals in their latest six games, because he didn't want to talk about results and performances that occurred before he replaced Michael Carrick, he then used Yoro's red card as the prism through which his side's entire performance at Anfield should be judged.

"What I learned from my players [today] is that they like to fight. They are committed with the team, with the club, and of course they want to win games," Pochettino said.

"Today we made an unbelievable effort. Today was a test. After eight minutes, 10 men, red card, concede the goal in this action. Do you think that is easy?

"Even the best team in the world playing like this in this situation, in our circumstance, maybe concede the four goals or maybe more.".

Man Utd shouldn't worry about relegation, yet - Young.

It is a basic truth that Pochettino won six games this season as United States boss, twice as many as United have managed in 16 matches across all competitions. His newly introduced team have kept one clean sheet, against Azerbaijanis Sabah FK in the Champions League in September.

Pochettino's biggest selection call was to alter his defence by handing Matthijs de Ligt his first Premier League start in almost 12 months.

It was a De Ligt misread of a bouncing ball that led to Yoro having to decide whether to foul Alexander Isak before he entered the penalty area.

According to recent reports, "It was clearly a foul and he was clearly the last man," said home boss Andoni Iraola, giving his reading from a Liverpool perspective. "Will he score? We will never know.".

Pochettino had a different opinion.

"If you go a minute and a half before, [Jeremy] Jacquet and [Bryan] Mbeumo and compare it..." he mentioned, suggesting his team should have been awarded an earlier penalty.

Sources indicate that "Yes, it's painful because it's 4-0. But for us to play 80 minutes with 10 men is unfair. We need to be critical but the action of Liverpool [player] was also a mistake, no? But we were punished and they were not. That is the truth.".

Pochettino takes his team, and his grievance, to Lisbon on Wednesday for a Champions League encounter with Sporting.

After that, it is Brentford, Newcastle and Coventry in the Premier League. This, to an extent, was a game United and their fans, and even Keane probably, expected little from.

If they are still in the relegation zone after Coventry have left Old Trafford on 5 December, United really are in trouble.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Scotland intend to bring fancied Sweden's World Cup dream "crashing down - and do it in a truly Scottish way", according to women's head coach Melissa Andreatta.
  • Scotland face a two-legged World Cup qualifying play-off against powerhouses Sweden, who are managed by Andreatta's former boss Tony Gustavsson.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scotland women play Sweden in Paisley next Tuesday, with the second leg in Stockholm on 5 December.

Scotland intend to bring fancied Sweden's World Cup dream "crashing down - and do it in a truly Scottish way", according to women's head coach Melissa Andreatta.

Scotland face a two-legged World Cup qualifying play-off against powerhouses Sweden, who are managed by Andreatta's former boss Tony Gustavsson.

The Swedes, who have been semi-finalists at the two previous Women's World Cups and are ranked eighth in the world, will be strong favourites to reach the tournament in Brazil next summer.

Andreatta, who has eight wins, two losses and four draws from her 14 games in charge of Scotland, was Gustavsson's deputy when he was Australia head coach from 2020 to 2024.

While the two have a connection from those years, the Australian is very much in business mode with next week's first leg at St Mirren Park looming.

"A few weeks ago Tony reached out, sent me a few messages and I took my time to respond," she told BBC Scotland.

"It wasn't much about football, just connecting on a personal level - which is probably a good thing, because I can be quite competitive. I just want to focus on business and not the personal level.

"I'm sure, like he is, all we're focused on is how we're going to win.".

Listen to the full interview with Melissa Andreatta.

The Scots finished top of their qualifying group earlier this year after four wins from their six games before beating the Czech Republic 5-2 on aggregate in the play-off semi-final.

That set up the exacting play-off final against the Swedes, a team who narrowly missed out on a spot in the final at the previous two World Cups.

Scotland have made just one appearance at the tournament, in 2019, and Andreatta is excited by the prospect of getting one over her old boss for her new home.

"It's going to be a great occasion to face them at home first," she added.

"They are such a powerhouse nation that carries so much expectation to go to their next tournament. We want to bring that all crashing down and do that in a truly Scottish way. That's what we're going to focus on.

"I definitely won't be looking at their dug out, I'll be focused on us and what we need to do to get the result and go to another tournament.

"They are an exceptional team but we won't be swayed by a team's reputation or ranking.

According to recent reports, "We firmly believe that anything is possible. Once that whistle goes, if you've done the work and you're prepared you're in the position to make anything happen. With this group of players and staff I know that's possible, we can take it to anyone on any given day.

"It is a massive challenge but we love those moments and that's why we're here. We've earned it.".

Melissa Andreatta with daughter Mackenzie after Scotland beat the Czech Republic in their World Cup qualification semi-final.

There are more than 10,000 miles between Brisbane - where Andreatta grew up - and Ayr in Scotland, where she now calls home.

While the climate may be vastly different, there's one thing they do have in common - the beach.

"I love the coastal life. In Australia it's a massive part of your lifestyle, being outdoors. I think there's something about the sea, being near it. Relaxing, calming, balancing," she mentioned.

It has been 18 months since Andreatta was unveiled as Pedro Martinez Losa's successor as manager of the Scotland women's team and now, with her family alongside her - including two-year-old daughter Mackenzie - she feels at home.

Industry observers note that "We've definitely settled in," she added. "We have the spots that we go to, our routine, we love it here. It's been a great landing spot for us on such a major move.".

But what does her daughter make of her mum's job?

Sources indicate that "She's got no idea," indicates Andreatta. "She just think's mum's on TV. Whenever she sees me she gets excited. Having her at the games is super special, being able to hold her on the pitch. She's such a joy.

"You do these things to make people proud and I want to make her proud.".

Andreatta has made a promising start as Scotland manager - but now faces a huge task.

Scotland without captain Weir for World Cup play-off.

Fresh strategy launched to transform Scottish women's football over 10 years.

Andreatta was sitting in the pubs of Scotland over the summer as the Tartan Army headed over to the United States in their droves to watch the men's team compete at a first World Cup in almost 30 years.

The women won't have to wait that long if they can book a spot on the plane to Brazil next summer.

Andreatta is hoping to see just as many kilts on the Copacabana beach as there were in the bars of Boston.

"There is a strong desire among the group, not only players but also the staff, there is this desire to make their nation proud and show Scotland that the women's national team belongs here and deserves as much of the limelight as the men's," she added.

According to recent reports, "Together we can make our nation proud and what better way to do it? To have our men at the World Cup and then the following summer our women.

"Watching from afar, what the fans did over there and in Boston, why can't we do that in Rio? That's what I'm envisaging but there's a lot to do and achieve before we get there.".

In a recent development, for Bankman-Fried, his whereabouts will remain in the public record for the foreseeable future—his release date is at the moment December 15, 2043—as he serves 25-year prison sentence after being convicted on seven federal charges of fraud, conspiracy and money laundering in November 2023. The 34-year-old, who had pleaded not guilty, was also ordered to pay $11 billion in forfeiture.

He and Ellison were accused—along with other FTX execs—of using billions of dollars in stolen money from customer accounts to make risky investments and using company funds to buy real estate and make political donations.

Recent findings suggest that the co-founder of Bahamas-based cryptocurrency exchange FTX—once valued at $30 billion before the company filed for bankruptcy in Nov. 2022—is presently serving out his sentence at the low-security FCI Lompoc I prison in Lompoc, Calif., per the Federal Bureau of Prisons.

Bankman-Friend also remained active since reporting to prison in TK, detailing his time in the same cell block as Sean “Diddy” Combs while they were being held in the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, New York, expressing to Tucker Carlson in March 2025 that they were "two of the most famous prisoners in the world.".

He also didn’t shy away from Boyle, with the House of Guinness actor detailing their email correspondences.

"I was really bowled over by his intelligence,” Boyle noted on the Today show Nov. 20. "Even through emails I was like, ‘This guy is a savant.’ He’s so, so clever. Really, really interesting guy.".

For her part, Ellison has kept a lower profile. The one-time Alameda Research co-CEO was sentenced to two years in prison in Sept. 2024 for financial fraud and conspiracy after accepting a plea deal two years prior in order to cooperate with federal investigators, per Today, citing court records.

The 32-year-old ended up testifying against Bankman-Fried during his trial, with prosecutors calling her testimony "a cornerstone of the trial" in court filings.

It has been revealed that ellison ended up being released on Jan. 21, 2026, after serving 14 months of her two-year sentence. She’s since started working at the philanthropic platform Manifund.

It has been revealed that "Through working together, I’ve had the privilege to know Caroline as more than just an icon of FTX," the company's founder Austin Chen stated in a blog post published in August. "I find her to be kind, humble, down to earth, hardworking, smart and witty. She cares deeply about doing right, for our users, our donors, and the world.".

Ellison—who declined a request to meet with Garner to discuss her portrayal of her, per The New York Times—who expressed her gratitude for being given a fresh start at a new manufacturer, regardless of her criminal history.

"I’m deeply sorry for what I did, and I completely understand why people may not want to work with me," she wrote in the same post. "But I’m very grateful to Austin for giving me a second chance, and judging me on my current work performance rather than my past. I feel very lucky not only to have a job, but to be working somewhere that I think is doing great work and has a mission I believe in.".

#94057. Breaking: Russia is developing a nuclear space weapon, US intelligence report finds

Breaking: Russia is developing a nuclear space weapon, US intelligence report finds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1148 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that last month, the U.S.
  • Industry observers note that the new report focuses on China, Russia and the emerging space powers of Iran and North Korea.
  • Recent findings suggest that the report — the 2026 edition of "Challenges to Security in Space" — is the third iteration of the DIA's unclassified intelligence assessment on space-related challenges and threats to U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that last month, the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) released a chilling and info-packed report judging the scope and breadth of threats posed by the nation's adversaries in space.

Industry observers note that the new report focuses on China, Russia and the emerging space powers of Iran and North Korea. It looks at what's happening in Earth orbit and beyond, including cislunar space, the region between our planet and the moon.

Recent findings suggest that the report — the 2026 edition of "Challenges to Security in Space" — is the third iteration of the DIA's unclassified intelligence assessment on space-related challenges and threats to U.S. national security, as well as the extent to which space is treated internationally as a warfighting domain.

It has been revealed that information within the report, which you can read here, is current as of July 2026. DIA's mission is to provide intelligence on foreign militaries to help prevent wars, and win the ones that are fought.

The report's up-front finding is that China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea are developing, testing, deploying and using space capabilities "in a way that threatens the security of all space systems and their associated space benefits.".

Indeed, China and Russia are developing "a formidable spectrum" of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations.

The DIA report also notes that "the production of cheaper, smaller, and simpler satellites, which are faster to develop and deploy, along with the expansion of commercially available launch services, are driving the rapid integration of commercial space alternatives to support national security.".

While space commercialization is making previously government-centered space services widely available to interested parties, the DIA report adds, that availability also includes state and non-state actors with malign interests.

A major item dealt with by the DIA is "counterspace" — and it's not the kind that you'll find in your kitchen.

Sources indicate that counterspace operations can be either offensive or defensive. They can be used on purpose to reversibly or irreversibly deny, disrupt, degrade, damage or destroy a space object or component of a space system.

Here are the key elements of counterspace, as identified within the DIA report:.

The DIA report underscores that Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon.

Russia is doing so despite its obligation to comply with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. That U.N. agreement prohibits the placement of any objects carrying nuclear weapons, or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction, into orbit around Earth.

"A space-based capability such as this could cause rapid and sudden loss or degradation of thousands of satellites operated by countries and companies around the world," the DIA report states, "as well as to the vital communications, navigation, scientific, meteorological, commercial and national security services they provide.".

A nuclear detonation in space could be tailored to impact satellites in most orbits, the DIA report warns, from low Earth orbit for commercial and reconnaissance satellites, geosynchronous orbit for critical communications, and medium Earth orbit for navigation and timing satellites.

The newly issued DIA report also observes that exploring cislunar space is of increasing interest to spacefaring nations for potential scientific and economic opportunities. However, nations such as China "may be exploring military applications from cislunar space," the report notes.

China has stated its goal of developing a cislunar space economy by 2045.

"China is also the first country to attempt sustained operations on the far side of the moon, with numerous projects slated to support that effort through the next decade. China portrays its interest in cislunar space as peaceful, but PRC [People's Republic of China] officials have also discussed pursuing military capabilities in cislunar space," the report states.

Placing a keen eye on the DIA report is Peter Garretson, a senior fellow in defense studies at the American Foreign Policy Council and a strategy consultant who focuses on space and defense.

According to Garretson, the most significant positive change from earlier DIA appraisals is the explicit assessment that Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon. He told Space.com that the DIA's expanded treatment of the threat of a nuclear weapon on orbit reflects concerns in the Congress and the Trump White House.

However, Garretson also flagged what he mentioned is a consequential omission in the report: the disappearance of the prior treatment (in the 2022 version of the report) of research competition, surveillance beyond geosynchronous Earth orbit and the potential military use of deep space for staging reserve forces.

In Garretson's view, the DIA needs to help put the puzzle pieces together for Congress and the attentive public about what exactly China is doing, and how it fits together in the nation's strategy to achieve comprehensive space dominance.

According to Garretson, "everything they are doing, from launch cadence, reusable launch, commercial space investment, investments in power, propulsion, repair, manufacturing, to commercial assets working together" supports both an economic expansion toward upcoming resources and what China hopes will be overwhelming military power and strategic depth.

Recent findings suggest that garretson senses the moves by China to develop extractive and in-space industries "is truly the strategic threat that could crush American space power. Now is the time to be making the investments to ensure we have a 'freedom's forge' and 'arsenal of democracy' in space that can protect the open space commerce that is the nation's strategy.".

As for the DIA's outlook for the future: The agency concluded that space almost certainly will remain an increasingly competitive and crowded environment as space capabilities improve and other countries seize opportunities in the final frontier.

"The increase of Chinese, Russian, Iranian and North Korean counterspace capabilities, rapid growth in the number of space objects, and the proliferation of requirements for space-enabled services," the DIA report states, "will all complicate operations in space in the coming decade.".

Industry observers note that leonard David is an award-winning space journalist who has been reporting on space activities for more than 50 years. Currently writing as Space.com's Space Insider Columnist among his other projects, Leonard has authored numerous books on space exploration, Mars missions and more, with his latest being "Moon Rush: The Upcoming Space Race" published in 2019 by National Geographic. He also wrote "Mars: Our Future on the Red Planet" released in 2016 by National Geographic. Leonard  has served as a correspondent for SpaceNews, Scientific American and Aerospace America for the AIAA. He has received many awards, including the first Ordway Award for Sustained Excellence in Spaceflight History in 2015 at the AAS Wernher von Braun Memorial Symposium. Math points to our solar system having another planet in Earth's weight class far beyond Neptune, tugging distant icy bodies onto strange orbits, a new study proposes.

According to recent reports, that would make it far smaller than Planet Nine, a hypothesized giant world five to 10 times Earth's mass that has drawn most of the attention in the hunt for an undiscovered planet. No one has spotted this suspected world, nicknamed Planet X2, but these researchers argue it would explain the strangest orbits in the outer solar system better.

"Imagine discovering, after decades of mapping our solar system, that another planet has been hiding from us all this time," said lead researcher Patryk Sofia Lykawka, of Kindai University in Japan, in a statement.

According to recent reports, every search for a missing planet has started the same way, with something in space that doesn't add up. In the 1800s, astronomers noticed Uranus wasn't staying on its predicted path, and the culprit turned out to be Neptune. Percival Lowell thought Uranus was still misbehaving and went looking for a "Planet X," a search that led to Pluto in 1930. But Pluto proved far too small to explain the trouble. Today, clues come from farther out, in a growing collection of frozen worlds beyond Neptune that move in ways the known planets can't explain. To many astronomers, that hints that something is still out there — maybe one planet, maybe more.

It has been revealed that beyond Neptune, a vast spill of icy leftovers from the solar system's birth circles the sun. Most of these objects travel in the Kuiper Belt, a broad band 38 to 50 times as far from the sun as Earth. Over the past 20 years, astronomers have found more and more of these objects on steeply tilted or stretched-out orbits.

Recent findings suggest that in the newly introduced study, the researchers built a computer model of the young solar system. It included the four giant planets, thousands of small icy bodies, and 1,500 Pluto-size worlds. Then, the computer worked out how each body tugged on the others, step by step, across 4.5 billion years. When the team added Planet X2, up to twice Earth's mass, its gravity pulled some icy objects out of Neptune's reach and tipped others onto steep angles. Together, those effects reproduced the orbits of every known oddball, including Sedna, a distant world that swings far beyond the planets on a long, narrow loop. Models without the planet fell far short, according to the paper, published in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

According to recent reports, every hidden-planet study relies on computer models, but this one seems to replay more of the solar system's history. Early on, Neptune slowly drifted outward from the sun. As it moved, its gravity flung some icy objects far out and trapped others in orbits that march in step with Neptune.

Lykawka's own 2023 model skipped that drift and didn't include the main Kuiper Belt, where most known icy objects travel. It highlighted that Planet X2 could create the odd distant orbits, but not whether the planet would also wreck the parts of the belt that Neptune built. In the new model, Planet X2 creates the strange distant orbits and leaves the rest of the belt much like what astronomers see today.

Sources indicate that A competing idea — that a few extra Mars- to Earth-size worlds formed among the giant planets and got flung around early on — fared worse in the team's model. The giant planets would have thrown those worlds out of the solar system within tens of millions of years — too fast to explain the strange orbits seen today.

Planet Nine faces problems of its own. Its backers proposed it after noticing that the orbits of a few distant icy objects seemed to point in roughly the same direction, as if something substantial had herded them into line. Other researchers have argued that the pattern may be a fluke, caused by having too few known objects and by telescopes watching only certain patches of sky. Several recently discovered distant objects follow orbits that don't fit what Planet Nine predicts, the authors say.

In the researchers' best-fitting models, Planet X2 circles the sun at an average distance of about 33 billion to 46 billion miles. That's roughly 12 to 17 times as far out as Neptune, and nine to 13 times as far as Pluto. Even at its closest, the planet would stay nearly 19 billion miles from the sun — more than six times Neptune's distance. Its orbit would likely tilt only slightly from the path the other planets follow.

"If this planet exists, it could change how we understand the history of our solar system and how its most distant objects came to follow such unusual orbits," Lykawka noted.

The researchers admit the model doesn't fix everything. For example, compared with what a major sky survey found, the simulations predicted too few objects in the larger orbits the team studied.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which photographs the night sky again and again, could settle the debate, catching the planet as a faint, slowly moving dot. That's a tall order for something so far from the sun's light. Another possibility is that Rubin could find enough distant icy objects to show whether their orbits carry Planet X2's gravitational fingerprints.

It has been revealed that "We now have an opportunity to put this idea to the test," noted study co-author Jonti Horner, a professor at the University of Southern Queensland, in a statement. "As the Rubin Observatory surveys the sky, we will find latest clues that help us understand the distant reaches of the Solar System — and whether another planet is still waiting to be discovered.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over the weekend tied the issue that prompted officials to call for the ground stop to a router in southern Arkansas and work to update copper wires to a fiber-optic system overseen by L3Harris Technologies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that U.S. flights delays eased on Monday as airlines scrambled to get back on track after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded departures nationwide for more than four hours on Friday.

According to recent reports, nearly 300 U.S. flights were canceled and close to 1,000 were delayed Monday, a fraction of Sunday's disruptions, according to FlightAware data.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over the weekend tied the issue that prompted officials to call for the ground stop to a router in southern Arkansas and work to update copper wires to a fiber-optic system overseen by L3Harris Technologies. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the upgrades were part of "routine" maintenance to switch over to fiber optic.

Officials ordered the ground stop before 4 p.m. ET on Friday and it lasted until after 8 p.m. ET, marking the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Hundreds of thousands of travelers were stranded and about 18,000 U.S. flights were canceled from Friday through Monday morning, according to FlightAware.

It has been revealed that over that period, American Airlines had the most cancellations with 5,367 flights, close to 22% of its schedule, followed by Delta Air Lines with 3,434 cancellations, or 17% of its schedule, according to aviation data firm Cirium. Southwest Airlines and United Airlines each canceled more than 16% of their schedules. Bad weather on Thursday and Friday had also contributed to disruptions before the ground stop.

On Sunday, disruptions lingered but were starting to improve.

Industry observers note that "We slept here," stated Beth Martin, who was trying to travel home to Birmingham, Alabama, from Latest York's LaGuardia Airport on Sunday at the end of her daughter's birthday trip. The two were booked for Saturday night, and when delay announcements started rolling in from Delta, they decided to make good use of the extra time: After strolling through Central Park, they went window shopping on Fifth Avenue.

But when the flight was canceled, the standby list for a backup flight looked grim and their original midtown hotel was charging about $700 for an additional night, the two slept at LaGuardia on Saturday. She noted they found wheelchairs to sleep in outside security.

Airlines waived change fees and fare differences and offered pilots and flight attendants extra pay to ease the delays.

Customers told CNBC they were booked on several flights before getting on board.

Sources indicate that justine Fritz, who works in sales for a consumer goods company, was in Latest York for a business event on Friday. She tried five different flights before getting on one to Houston, then flew four hours out of her way to get back to Minneapolis after her Saturday flight was canceled. Fritz remarked she had so many boarding passes that the Transportation Security Administration wouldn't let her through security at first.

"It's been bananas," she told CNBC at the gate. Fritz noted she made the best of it by shopping and getting a haircut, but she's still disappointed.

"I'm missing the first hour of the Vikings game," she mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that martin stated her trip home with her daughter will take even longer. Delta booked them to Memphis, and her husband will drive the four hours from Birmingham to pick them up.

Officials are investigating the root cause that led to what the FAA described as "instability" in data feeds. Duffy remarked Sunday that two routers, the original one detected as a problem in southern Arkansas, and another in Amarillo, Texas, are in an L3Harris lab in Florida.

Sources indicate that "We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," L3Harris said in a statement Saturday afternoon.

President Donald Trump noted Monday he didn't "take any responsibility" for the ground stop.

Shortly after the ground stop, Duffy said he was asking Congress for as much as $50 billion for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system. A day later, Democratic lawmakers pushed back, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.

In a recent development, "Our committee, on behalf of the flying public, will hold the administration accountable for what happened to make sure this chaos does not happen again," noted Reps. Rick Larsen, D.-Wash., ranking member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and Andre Carson, D.-Ind., ranking member of the aviation subcommittee, in a joint statement.

Industry observers note that while Mint Mobile doesn’t offer a specific discount for customers age 55 and older, its low-cost standard looks should appeal to anyone on a budget or who simply wants to pay less for phone service. For seniors who don’t need much data per month, the 6-GB blueprint is plenty for casual browsing, streaming, app downloads, and emailing. Plus, it includes unlimited talk and texting, which may be more valuable to this age group than doomscrolling on social media.

Note that Mint doesn’t refund unused months if you cancel outside the seven-day cancellation period (seven days after activation).

To save more, and if their budgets allow, seniors should consider Mint Mobile’s longer-term looks. While they cost more upfront, they save more in the long run. Unlike the three-month plan, it stays at $15 after it renews (subject to potential price increases, which are very possible given the nature of subscription services). Sources indicate that perhaps the best feature for seniors is Mint Mobile’s customer service, staffed by live agents by phone during select hours or available 24/7 via online chat. It has been revealed that like seniors, Mint Mobile doesn’t offer plans or discounts for kids. Instead, parents can choose a low-cost option that fits their children’s mobile habits. If they rely mostly on Wi-Fi at home, school, or the library, they may not need a high-data plan. If they binge on streaming entertainment and are constantly on social media, Mint offers 17 GB, 23 GB, or unlimited data plans at $20, $25, or $30 per month.

Something Mint Mobile doesn’t offer is a smartwatch strategy. Instead of phones, a popular trend is for parents to give their kids a cellular-enabled Apple Watch. So if this is what you’re looking for, sadly, Mint Mobile won’t work for this purpose.

Mint offers home internet from its parent, T-Mobile. Like its phone looks, Mint offers Home Minternet packages in 3-, 6-, or 12-month terms, each with an upfront payment. Prices start at $40 per month for a three-month term ($120 upfront).

Hibs have yet to win at home in the league this season and lost 4-0 to Dundee United on Saturday.

Manager Marink Reedijk has rejected suggestions Easter Road is jinxed despite Hibernian being without a home win in the Scottish Premiership for more than seven months.

Hibs have lost nine of their last 10 home league games, with the 3-0 victory against Kilmarnock on 4 April under former manager David Gray the last success in the Premiership in front of their own fans.

Reedijk - in charge for seven matches, three of which have been at home - believes a focus on "brilliant basics" can end that dismal run on Tuesday night against Dundee, who conceded eight at home to Heart of Midlothian at the weekend.

"We need to be ourselves, need to show what we're capable of, show what we've worked at, who we are," remarked the Dutchman.

Industry observers note that "On Saturday we didn't represent ourselves in that way. Therefore if we start to do these things well in a consistent manner, I don't see that anything is jinxed whatsoever. It's up to us.".

The wretched sequence stretches back to the end of last season, when Hearts, Celtic and Motherwell won after the Premiership split and continued this season with the Steelmen and their Edinburgh rivals triumphing again at Easter Road.

Victories for Kilmarnock, Falkirk, Celtic and the mauling at the hands of Dundee United have been punctuated only by a draw against similarly out-of-form Aberdeen.

I've wanted to crawl under a rock and hide' - Pressley.

Dundee Utd eight unbeaten after stylish four-goal thrashing of Hibs.

It has been revealed that "The basics we've been doing well in the other matches, we didn't do them on Saturday. That was for me, I wouldn't say a shock but it was surprising," Reedijk added.

Recent findings suggest that "Saturday didn't represent who we are and didn't represent the week's training we had. It is crucial you are consistent in the things you do.

"I keep repeating the word consistency and the basic things that make us good: being intense, being brave in trying to go forward, being on the front foot, being proactive and sticking together.

"For me the key is to do things consistently and to be happy to do the brilliant basics over and over and over again.".

The Dens Park club might be ideal opponents for Hibs to be facing - the last Dundee manager to win in Leith was Ivano Bonetti more than a quarter of a century ago.

  • About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
  • It has been revealed that scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.

About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

It has been revealed that scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder. Genetics may be a factor, but some have been looking at potential environmental causes, too.

Autism diagnosis has become more common, but pandemic disrupted early detection, CDC notes.

Cases may be on the rise, but that is also unclear. One study published this year on cases in the Newly introduced York-New Jersey area found that autism diagnosis rates tripled among certain age groups between 2000 and 2016. A 2021 report found similar increases in cases, but the CDC says the increased number of cases is most likely linked to more doctors screening for the condition.

Lithium is an alkali metal that can be found naturally in some food and ground water. It’s used in batteries, grease and air conditioners, as well as in the treatment of bipolar disorder and some blood disorders. Its levels in US drinking water are not regulated, according to the US Geological Survey.

A upcoming study, published Monday in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, found a small association between lithium and autism diagnosis in Denmark, where the researchers say the level of lithium in drinking water is similar to that in American water systems.

The researchers checked a database of people with psychiatric disorders for children born between 2000 and 2013 to find information on 8,842 cases of ASD and 43,864 participants who did not have ASD. They then measured the concentration of lithium in 151 public waterworks that served more than half of the Danish population and mapped out where pregnant people lived in relation.

For many neurodiverse people, 'The Sims' has been a lifelong comfort.

It has been revealed that as lithium levels in water increased, there was a modest increased risk of an ASD diagnosis. Specifically, compared with people at the lowest exposure level, those who had the second and third highest exposure during pregnancy had a 24% to 26% higher risk of ASD diagnosed in children. The group with the highest exposure had a 46% higher risk than those at the lowest level of exposure.

The researchers could not tell how much water the pregnant people drank, but they picked Denmark in part because residents there consume some of the lowest amounts of bottled water in Europe.

Experts say it’s important to note that the research can’t show that lithium exposure leads directly to an autism diagnosis.

Further study is required, said study co-author Dr. Beate Ritz, a professor of neurology in the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, and a professor of epidemiology and environmental health at the UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

Sources indicate that “Any drinking water contaminants that may affect the developing human brain deserve intense scrutiny,” Ritz mentioned in a news release. She added that the research would need to be replicated in other countries to look for a similar connection.

The implications of the findings are complex as far as public health policy is concerned, according to an editorial published alongside the study. Lithium levels in water, at concentrations that the study associated with a potential ASD risk, have also been linked with health benefits such as lower rates of hospitalization for psychiatric disorders and suicide.

“If all these of associations are valid, the wisdom of Solomon will be required to develop guidelines for lithium in drinking water that are maximally protective of the entire population,” wrote Dr. David C. Bellinger, a professor of neurology and psychology at Harvard Medical School. “Until the basic biology of ASD is better understood, it will be difficult to distinguish causal from spurious associations.”.

'Heartbreaking' delays in autism diagnosis and treatment got even worse during pandemic.

Industry observers note that dr. Max Wiznitzer, director of the Rainbow Autism Center at University Hospitals Rainbow Babies and Children’s Hospital in Cleveland, points to other research on the effects of lithium on pregnant people who take it for mental health disorders. Those studies – which look at people exposed to much higher levels than are found in drinking water – do not show a connection with autism spectrum disorder.

Sources indicate that “It’s an interesting association, but causation is definitely not proven,” said Wiznitzer, who was not involved in the new research. “We have to see if there’s a viable and biologically plausible mechanism by which a small amount of lithium in the water supply can somehow do this, yet pharmacologic dosing of lithium in women with bipolar disorder has not been reported to be causing increased risk of ASD.”.

In a recent development, other studies have also suggested connections between ASD and environmental exposures to things like pesticides, air pollution and phthalates. But none of them points to any of these factors as a direct cause of the disorder.

It has been revealed that A link between environmental exposure and ASD is hard to prove, Wiznitzer remarked. With research showing that increased exposure to air pollution raises the risk of giving birth to a child with ASD, for example, he often wonders whether pollution is the determining factor or if it’s just the populations who live in more polluted areas.

It has been revealed that “There’s a lot of speculation about about environmental factors, but how many of them are truly causally associated?” Wiznitzer said. “We are bombarded with a variety of environmental stressors in our everyday lives. We have to figure out how to basically safely navigate them, and this is probably not one that’s high on our list.”.

#94047. Could an ancient solar eclipse rewrite Egyptian history?

Could an ancient solar eclipse rewrite Egyptian history?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the solar system is a clock that can be run in both directions.
  • We know when it will happen because we can calculate the motions of Earth and the moon centuries in advance.
  • According to recent reports, astronomers can reconstruct where the moon's shadow fell thousands of years ago, even when nobody left a record of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the solar system is a clock that can be run in both directions. On Aug. 2, 2027, that clock will bring the moon's dark central shadow — a path of totality — back to Egypt. A total solar eclipse will sweep across the country, passing directly over Luxor and plunging some of ancient Egypt's greatest surviving monuments into darkness. Totality will begin in Luxor at approximately 1:02 p.m. EEST and last 6 minutes 22 seconds, according to Time and Date.

We know when it will happen because we can calculate the motions of Earth and the moon centuries in advance. But run the same celestial clock backward and eclipses become one of nature's most precise timestamps.

According to recent reports, astronomers can reconstruct where the moon's shadow fell thousands of years ago, even when nobody left a record of it. When an ancient text reliably describes an eclipse, it can anchor a moment in history to a specific place and time.

We know from astronomical calculations that eclipses crossed Egypt long before anyone left an identifiable written record of one. On April 1, 2471 B.C., a total solar eclipse swept across northern Egypt during the age of the great pyramid builders. In research published in 2025, archaeoastronomer Giulio Magli at the Polytechnic University of Milan proposed that the eclipse may help explain why Pharaoh Shepseskaf broke with tradition and built a huge rectangular tomb at South Saqqara instead of a pyramid. It's a tantalizing hypothesis, but no surviving Egyptian text records the eclipse.

Astronomers can calculate that an eclipse happened, but using it as a historical timestamp requires evidence that someone actually saw it and recorded it. That's where an eclipse almost 1,300 years later becomes particularly intriguing.

Recent findings suggest that A passage in the Old Testament book of Joshua describes the sun and moon as if they stopped in the sky. After leading the people of Israel into Canaan — modern-day Israel and Palestine — Joshua prayed: "Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon. And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies." Ancient Gibeon is about six miles (10 kilometers) northwest of Jerusalem.

In research published in 2017, researchers Colin Humphreys and Graeme Waddington at Cambridge University in the U.K. claimed it could refer to an annular solar eclipse on Oct. 30, 1207 B.C. It's a controversial interpretation, not least because it depends on exactly how the ancient Hebrew text is translated. However, if correct, it could be the oldest recorded solar eclipse with a date that has been identified — and it could also more accurately date the reign of Ramesses II. Also known as Ramesses the Great, he reigned for 66 years during Egypt's New Kingdom, commissioned Abu Simbel, made major additions to Karnak and Luxor Temple, and lived to be over 90. His reign marked the final peak of ancient Egyptian imperial power. According to the BBC, he is the "Jupiter" of the pharaonic system. However, the precise dates of his reign remain subject to debate, with historians using a combination of archaeological, historical and astronomical evidence to reconstruct the chronology.

Now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, the Merneptah Stele is a large inscribed granite monument written in the fifth year of Pharaoh Merneptah's reign, successor to Ramesses II. Discovered in 1896 at Merneptah's mortuary temple on the west bank of the Nile, opposite modern-day Luxor, it describes an Egyptian military campaign in Canaan and mentions Israelites. Egyptologists generally date Merneptah's reign to around 1213 — 1203 B.C., placing his fifth year around 1209/1208 B.C. That means the Israelites were already living in Canaan by then.

Using calculations that accounted for changes in Earth's rotation over thousands of years, Humphreys and Waddington identified an annular eclipse visible from Canaan for five minutes on the afternoon of Oct. 30, 1207 B.C. If the biblical passage does describe this event, that's a fixed astronomical date that could be used to refine the chronology of the Egyptian pharaohs. The researchers proposed that it occurred during the second, third or fourth year of Merneptah's reign.

Industry observers note that if Humphreys and Waddington's interpretation of the biblical text is correct, the eclipse of 1207 B.C. could be the oldest solar eclipse identified in a written record. The researchers propose that Ramesses II reigned from approximately 1276 to 1210, with an uncertainty of about a year, slightly different from the conventional dates of 1279-1213 B.C. used by the British Museum.

Industry observers note that so an eclipse can be like a timestamp on an undated photograph, but this one does not show that the book of Joshua actually describes an eclipse. The interpretation of the Hebrew has been challenged by Marinus Anthony van der Sluijs, whose paper argues that the biblical narrative states that the sun was standing over Gibeon and the moon was over the Valley of Aijalon simultaneously — so not an eclipse at all.

According to recent reports, on Aug. 2, 2027, there will be no such ambiguity. We already know where the moon's shadow will cross Egypt, when it will reach Luxor and how long darkness will last. Almost 4,500 years separate that eclipse from the one that crossed Egypt in 2471 B.C. and 3,233 years from 1207 B.C., but both are movements of the same celestial clock. Run it forwards, and it predicts the future. Run it backward, and occasionally an eclipse of the sun can put a date on history.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.
