Manchester United lost 4-0 at Liverpool in their opening match under Mauricio Pochettino.

Manchester United's Premier League trip to Anfield was described by some as a free hit for latest head coach Mauricio Pochettino.

The theory was expectations for United were so low as they travelled to Liverpool that a positive outcome would be a huge bonus, and anything else was expected.

But Pochettino did not look like a man without pressure after 15 minutes of what turned into a 4-0 defeat.

By that point, his side were already 2-0 behind and down to 10 men. Liverpool's fans were gleefully singing about the Argentine being "sacked in the morning", even though he was only a sixth of the way through his first game in charge.

A day later, United supporters began filtering through Manchester Airport on their way to Lisbon for a Champions League match that marks the next stop in what has turned into a desperate campaign.

The prevailing mood was one of resigned acceptance punctuated by dark humour around what a season in the Championship might look like, and whether Manchester City might be there with them.

United's England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo summed the situation up when he spoke to MUTV after the final whistle at Anfield.

"We're at the lowest we've ever been and no-one's coming to save us," mentioned the 21-year-old.

"There are no helping hands coming, so we've got to work together, lean on each other, keep working and hopefully it will come good.

"It's all about character now.".

Pochettino has signed a two-and-a-half-year contract.

United are giving little away about their looks for the January transfer window.

For now, it is being stressed, Pochettino's priority is to get the most from the players presently at his disposal.

However, there was sympathy with former boss Michael Carrick's belief he had been let down in the summer window and there was a blueprint to address that.

Industry observers note that that situation remains. A striker is thought to be Pochettino's priority given United's only recognised number nine, Benjamin Sesko, is out at least until January with a shin issue that has bothered him since March.

United have a long-standing concern at left-back. First choice Luke Shaw missed his eighth successive game on Sunday and the only other orthodox left-back in senior ranks is England Under-20 international Harry Amass, who didn't even make the bench at Anfield.

However, Pochettino worked with Shaw at the start of his career at Southampton and feels the 31-year-old can be a positive influence on his group.

The reality though is United still have nine games to play before they can make any changes to their squad.

Among those fixtures are home games against Coventry, Nottingham Forest and Sunderland.

Newly promoted Coventry are four points ahead of United, who are second from bottom. Forest and Sunderland are in the two positions immediately above the Old Trafford club.

A trip to Crystal Palace - the one side below United, and the other Premier League club to replace their coach during the international break - looms on 13 December.

After Wednesday's encounter with Sporting, Pochettino's side have one Champions League game before the end of the year - against RB Leipzig on 8 December.

Sources indicate that any solutions to be found to the current mess over the next five weeks have to come from within. If they don't, light-hearted discussions about a first relegation since 1973-74 under Tommy Docherty start to get serious.

"They have got enough in that squad to get themselves out of the bottom three," Ashley Young - a Premier League winner with United - told Match of the Day.

"They have not been showing that, but Pochettino has only just come in. He is going to want to get his team set up in a way that they are hard to beat. Right now, they do not look like they are hard to beat.

Industry observers note that "It doesn't look like there is that togetherness. He has got to find a way to get that out of them. I am sure he will be able to do that when he has been longer in the job.".

Man Utd shouldn't worry about relegation right now - Young.

Pochettino shut down a question about United's terrible recent defensive record when he spoke to the media immediately after the game at Anfield.

"Tell me only about the circumstance today," he remarked. "I wasn't [here] in the past.".

That is true - and may also have been a useful diversion exercise in avoiding a dissection of a defensive unit he is still getting to know.

In a recent development, however, Pochettino knows United have kept one clean sheet all season - against Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK in September. He will also know United have now conceded 19 goals in their past six games.

Pochettino's major decision at Liverpool was to pick Matthijs de Ligt in the centre of a three-man defence ahead of Harry Maguire.

"He played in the Champions League you know, before the internationals," said the former Tottenham, PSG and Chelsea boss.

It was not clear when Pochettino meant.

Industry observers note that in the 4-1 loss at Como on 21 October, De Ligt made his first appearance in 11 months following major back problems that eventually required surgery, largely because Leny Yoro was suspended and Lisandro Martinez was injured. He then played for two minutes against Roma on 3 November, when he was thrown on as then manager Carrick searched desperately for a winner.

Most goals can be broken down into a number of mistakes that compound to make an eventual negative outcome.

Sources indicate that team positioning has been mentioned as a reason De Ligt found himself exposed under a high ball at Anfield. However, his failure to deal with it presented Alexander Isak with a clear run at goal and prompted Yoro to make the tackle that led to his controversial dismissal, which Pochettino felt shaped the 82 minutes that followed.

Sources indicate that but United have been conceding bad goals all season. Numerous players have been culpable.

Industry observers note that there is a limit to what Pochettino can do in the time available. However, he wants to maximise what he can do.

Whereas Carrick tended to let his starting players have a day off after matches, the upcoming regime has decided a warm-down session at Carrington is the better option.

And defensive organisation was surely one of the key points his coaching team had on their list of things to work on when the players began preparations to face Sporting on Wednesday.

Midfielder Andrey Santos has started three out of 10 Premier League games since the opening-day defeat at Hull.

With Â£70m summer arrival Carlos Baleba injured for the second time since the start of pre-season, Pochettino must find a way to protect United's goal, which might require additional support in midfield.

According to recent reports, the strengths of Mainoo and Youri Tielemans are with the ball. Either with three in the middle of defence or a third man in midfield, a way needs to be found to stop opposition attacks running straight at the defence.

In his recent interview with Sky Sports, United chief executive Omar Berrada said the club needed to be "disciplined" in the transfer market and avoid spending huge sums on players who would not necessarily make the squad better.

But the fact former Chelsea midfielder Andrey Santos went five games between Premier League starts under Carrick from the opening-day defeat at Hull - and was only introduced for the final three minutes at Anfield - suggests there are doubts over the Brazilian, who cost Â£48m in the summer.

Underneath that is the knowledge United borrowed from their revolving credit facility around all their major summer purchases and did the same again earlier this month when Pochettino was hired at a cost of just over Â£7.5m.

In public accounts released last week, United confirmed there was another Â£160m available in credit - but also they owe Â£417m in outstanding transfer fees, Â£236m of which is due within 12 months.

Neither before nor after the transfer window opens do any simple solutions to United's predicament present themselves.

Last season, fellow 'significant-six' club Tottenham did not save themselves until the final day of the season.

Confidence remains high at Old Trafford the situation will not be quite so dire for them, but it could be a very bumpy ride.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disney on Tuesday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that exceeded analysts' expectations and unveiled it's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029.

Those cost-cutting efforts include several rounds of layoffs announced in recent months, Disney's chief financial officer, Hugh Johnston, told CNBC. The most recent round, which seeks to reduce costs by up to 20%, was reported earlier this month.

Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston said, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs.".

Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro told investors on the company's earnings call that the job cuts are "not easy.".

Industry observers note that "They affect people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this firm," he said. "At the same time, these steps are notable if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment, and keeps investing in the content and technology that will drive our growth.".

The cuts will help Disney fund its $26 billion in projected content spend for fiscal 2027, a 9% increase from fiscal 2026.

The entertainment giant is also forecasting double-digit growth in earnings per share in the next fiscal year, as well as segment operating income growth of around 8%.

Disney noted that the majority of that growth will be concentrated in the first half of the year due to the theatrical debut of "Avengers: Doomsday" and a boost from the Super Bowl, which will air on Disney's ESPN and ABC networks.

Industry observers note that "The growth is really going to come in the first half of this year," Johnston noted. "That's the opposite of what we saw in '26, where the growth was backloaded.".

Sources indicate that the company will also increase its annual dividend to $2 a share, a 33% increase from the previously declared dividend. It will be payable in two installments of $1 per share, one in January and one in July.

Recent findings suggest that here's how Disney performed in its fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct. 3, compared with what Wall Street expected, according to LSEG:.

Disney reported net income for the fiscal fourth quarter of $2.61 billion, or $1.51 per share, compared with $1.31 billion, or 73 cents per share, during the same period the year prior.

Adjusting for one-time items, including severance and other restructuring charges as well as the value of intangible assets, Disney reported earnings per share of $1.77.

The manufacturer's revenue for the quarter was 16% higher year over year, and results were once again lifted by its parks and streaming divisions.

Industry observers note that disney's experiences segment, which includes its theme parks and cruises, reported nearly $10.11 billion in revenue, up 15% year over year. Operating income for the unit increased 20% to $2.25 billion.

The division is already a top performer for the organization, but it benefited in the fiscal fourth quarter because of an extra calendar week compared with the previous fiscal year.

While international attendance continues to lag at Disney's domestic parks, it is being offset by domestic attendance, especially at the Walt Disney World resort in Orlando, Florida, Johnston noted.

Recent findings suggest that growth at Disneyland Paris was driven by recent investments including an expansion area called World of Frozen. Attendance at the Hong Kong and Shanghai parks remained soft because of broad economic challenges in those regions, according to Disney.

Still, D'Amaro said he believes the growth in parks will be sustainable through next year, especially with new additions, including the "Monsters, Inc."-themed land "Monstropolis" opening at Walt Disney World in 2027.

"Q1 forward resort bookings at Walt Disney World are pacing up compared to the prior year," he said. "And upcoming capacity and new experiences will start coming online in 2027. We keep investing to make the experience fresh, and what we see is that drives repeat visits.".

Industry observers note that the company expects operating income for the experiences segment to grow in the high-single digits in fiscal 2027. Growth is expected to be front-loaded as the company laps the launch of the Disney Adventure cruise ship, which set sail in March.

Over at its entertainment division, Disney saw revenue increase 17% to $11.89 billion. Operating income nearly doubled to $1.33 billion.

Revenue from streaming, specifically, rose 19% to $6.1 billion, Disney said.

The segment benefited from the extra week on the fiscal calendar as well as from growth in subscription and affiliate fees. Additionally, the company saw higher theatrical distribution revenue from titles like "Toy Story 5.".

Disney said Tuesday it expects operating income for the entertainment division to grow in the high-single digits in the coming fiscal year.

The company's sports division saw revenue increase 16% in the fiscal fourth quarter, reaching $4.61 billion. Operating income for the segment surged more than 50% to $1.39 billion.

Subscription and affiliate fees fueled this growth alongside an increase in advertising revenue.

In a recent development, the firm expects its sports division's operating income to grow by double digits in fiscal 2027. It noted that the fiscal first quarter of the year will see some declines because of the timing of College Football Playoff games and the New Year's window. However, the fiscal second quarter will benefit from the college championship as well as the broadcast of Super Bowl 61.

Disney's outlook for overall and segment results for fiscal 2027 excludes the impact of a 53rd week in fiscal 2026.

Sources indicate that D'Amaro has made advancing technology a pillar of the company's growth strategy. In September, Disney hired Karandeep Anand in the newly created position of chief technology officer.

"Technology is central to how we connect fans to more of Disney and drive returns on our investment," D'Amaro said on the earnings call. "[Anand has] been energized by how much opportunity he sees to move faster and go further in product and technology. Done right, that means serving our fans even better, working more efficiently and being more innovative across every one of our businesses.".

Disney unveiled a partnership with Adobe earlier this month to develop generative artificial intelligence models.

D'Amaro told investors that the team is exploring ways to use AI to make booking trips to Disney parks easier.

"There's actually a vacation planning tool that's in beta right now at Walt Disney World. We built that with our partners at Google, and I've had a chance to experiment with it myself," he remarked. "It'll be incredibly helpful for our guests who are booking trips. With these AI features, it can feel like you've got someone sitting right by your side, like a personal concierge, that plans and responds to the way that you want to actually book your trip to Walt Disney World.".

Sources indicate that the entertainment company has also expanded its short-form content, adding a vertical video channel within the Disney+ mobile app. The company had previously announced a partnership with TikTok to bring creator content to the streaming app.

Breaking: Continuous N-to-C Peptide Synthesis

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (596 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, current state-of-the-art peptide synthesis faces a significant global challenge in efficiency and sustainability.1 With demand for peptide therapeutics growing rapidly,2,3 our ability to provide these important medicines is under increasing pressure.4 Chemical synthesis typically proceeds C-to-N and requires protecting groups, whereas ribosomal synthesis proceeds N-to-C from unprotected amino acids (AAs).
  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, current state-of-the-art peptide synthesis faces a significant global challenge in efficiency and sustainability.1 With demand for peptide therapeutics growing rapidly,2,3 our ability to provide these important medicines is under increasing pressure.4 Chemical synthesis typically proceeds C-to-N and requires protecting groups, whereas ribosomal synthesis proceeds N-to-C from unprotected amino acids (AAs). To improve efficiency and sustainability, we developed a continuous N-to-C Peptide Synthesis (NCPS) using N-/C-unprotected AAs or fragments without intermediate isolations, achieving ≥95% average yield per coupling and ≤1.0% epimerization. The method enabled seven consecutive couplings. Starting from N-/C-unprotected AAs, peptide assembly requires fewer isolations than those needed to prepare the corresponding Fmoc-AA building blocks before conventional synthesis can begin. This method accepts all 20 canonical AAs and a wide range of non-canonical AAs important for drug-like profiles.5 Longer peptides can be readily assembled through continuous fragment coupling while maintaining chiral integrity. This approach reduces isolations by ~10-fold and waste generation by up to ~100-fold. We further developed a flow synthesizer that enhances speed and productivity while mitigating batch manufacturing risks. The method enabled the synthesis of a tirzepatide heptapeptide fragment, degarelix, a 14-mer engineered macrocyclic peptide, and semaglutide. Overall, continuous NCPS has the potential to transform peptide manufacturing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's plans to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.

But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.

"We are extremely concerned about the situation," stated a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.

Recent findings suggest that the IPCC's scientific assessments, published every six to seven years, provide the basis for major international climate agreements, including the 2015 Paris Agreement. The IPCC began evaluating the latest climate science in 1988 and its most recent report was published in 2023.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Researchers should have actually already started work on the next edition but the last plenary session was put on hold in October at the urging of Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and Kenya.

"The IPCC finds itself in a difficult situation," a spokesperson from the German Environment Ministry told DW at COP. "We stand ready to help resolve this concern, so that the panel can continue its work. To that end, we are holding many discussions with various countries to explore possible solutions.".

At the core of the dispute is the question of whether future UN climate talks base their negotiations on the latest scientific knowledge — or not.

That's especially relevant for the next "global stocktake," due in 2028, a report card on the world's climate efforts, which will shape action aims for countries around the world to lower planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.

In a recent development, the European Union, Brazil, the United Kingdom, small island states and several other countries especially at risk of the effects of climate change have called for the IPCC's seventh assessment report to be published in 2028, so it can be used to inform next steps for climate action. The report covers climate protection and impact.

It has been revealed that "It's much more difficult without these scientific reports. Otherwise, we're just talking to ourselves or relying on information that's no longer current," stated a delegation source.

But Russia, Iran, India and Saudi Arabia want the IPCC report postponed until 2029, after the global stocktake.

The official reason: the tight timeline would be detrimental to the quality of the research, and could hinder the participation of researchers and governments representing developing countries.

Disagreements over budget concerns have also held up the IPCC's work. Among other expenses, the funds are used to pay the travel arrangements for the hundreds of volunteer scientists, especially those from poorer countries, to attend the IPCC sessions.

"No budget means no more IPCC," noted a member from another delegation, also speaking on condition of anonymity.

It hasn't come to that point yet, but without planning certainty the whole process risks being delayed — along with the climate negotiations that depend on this knowledge.

Researchers with the IPCC, however, have said the timeline is attainable.

According to recent reports, "We have no time to lose," remarked an open letter released in October signed by more than 100 researchers from 36 countries — including India and China. "We stand committed to continue working to deliver the [seventh assessment report] in a manner that is rigorous, timely and inclusive.".

But while the dispute over the timeline won't alter the scientific findings themselves, it could delay their political impact.

In its pre-COP communications, France accused the countries delaying the report's publication schedule of attempting to "obstruct science in order to lower the ambition of the global stocktake.".

The IPCC isn't a stranger to attempts at political persuasion: At past climate conferences, delegates from many countries have regularly negotiated the exact phrasing of the summary reports intended for policymakers.

Speaking at COP31 on November 17, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said it was "fundamental to protect the integrity of climate science and the role of the IPCC as the source of best available science.".

Although there is no vote on the IPCC at COP31, it's possible that its significance and a timeline for the next report will be included in the final declaration of the climate talks, expected this weekend.

The IPCC has been warning for years that disinformation is hindering global climate action. And the struggle for information and control over the narrative in Antalya hasn't just been limited to the IPCC.

This was apparent in a document DW obtained that had been sent anonymously to several less wealthy countries' delegations in the run-up to COP31.

It claimed to explain the nature of Turkey's proposed goals for boosting electrification to 35% by 2035, but went on to misrepresent several core details of the aims to make them seem less appealing to developing countries than they are in reality.

At least two countries confirmed to DW that they had received the document. It did not state where it hailed from and was labeled as an "equity assessment.".

The presentation portrays electrification as a business venture undertaken by wealthy countries at the expense of poorer nations. The International Energy Agency, however, has calculated that developing countries could save around $100 billion (€90 billion) in fossil fuel imports by 2035 through electrification.

Sources indicate that the presentation also gives the impression that all countries must meet fixed electrification targets. In fact, according to the UN, the 35% target represents a global goal, with individual countries free to determine their own national pathways.

This article was originally written in German.

Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A consistent daily routine may do more for your health than you realize.
  • The findings suggest that everyday habits, such as waking up, eating meals, socializing, and going to bed at consistent times, may play an important role in physical and mental well-being.
  • Industry observers note that the discovery could be especially crucial for older adults, who frequently experience sleep difficulties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A consistent daily routine may do more for your health than you realize. Researchers at the University of Missouri have found that older adults who follow regular daily schedules tend to experience less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggle to get a good night's sleep.

The findings suggest that everyday habits, such as waking up, eating meals, socializing, and going to bed at consistent times, may play an important role in physical and mental well-being. By helping the body maintain its natural internal clock, a predictable routine could offer health benefits that extend beyond improved sleep.

Industry observers note that the discovery could be especially crucial for older adults, who frequently experience sleep difficulties. According to the National Council on Aging, roughly half of adults age 60 and older report symptoms of insomnia, a condition that can make it difficult to fall asleep, stay asleep, or get restful sleep.

Daily Routines Linked to Less Pain and Depression.

To investigate the relationship between sleep, daily habits, and overall health, Eunjin Tracy, an assistant professor in the College of Education and Human Development at the University of Missouri, examined survey responses from 67 older adults. Among the participants, 37 reported experiencing insomnia.

In a recent development, as researchers expected, those with insomnia generally reported more physical pain and higher levels of depression than participants without the condition. However, another pattern emerged when Tracy examined their daily routines.

Participants who maintained more consistent schedules tended to report less pain and fewer depressive symptoms, regardless of their sleep quality. This suggests that keeping regular daily habits may be associated with better health even when sleep problems persist.

"Regardless of sleep quality, those who reported having a regular daily routine had lower levels of physical pain and less depression compared to those without a daily routine," Tracy mentioned. "If we are consistent with when we wake up, eat, work or study, interact with others and go to bed, those time cues help synchronize our internal body clocks. Over the long term, that seems to be linked with improved health outcomes.".

Why Your Body's Internal Clock Matters.

Sources indicate that one possible explanation involves the circadian rhythm, the body's natural 24-hour timing system. This internal clock helps coordinate when we feel awake or sleepy and influences numerous biological processes, including hormone activity, metabolism, and mood.

Rather than operating independently of our surroundings, the circadian system responds to signals that help it keep time. Light and darkness are especially important, but regular activities such as eating, working, interacting with others, and sleeping can also provide timing cues.

Sources indicate that when these signals follow a predictable pattern, they help keep the body's biological rhythms aligned. Irregular schedules, on the other hand, can interfere with that coordination.

"When we regulate our circadian rhythm well, our bodies function well, but if it gets too distracted, our bodies don't function as well," Tracy said.

Although the study did not establish that regular routines directly reduce pain or depression, the findings point to circadian regulation as one possible explanation for the connection.

The Hidden Effects of Social Jet Lag.

Even relatively small changes in daily schedules may disrupt the body's internal clock. One common example is social jet lag, which occurs when a person's sleep schedule shifts between workdays and days off.

Someone who wakes up early throughout the week but stays up late and sleeps in on weekends may experience this mismatch. The resulting disruption resembles some of the effects of traveling across time zones, even though the person has never left home.

Tracy suggests that maintaining reasonably consistent schedules throughout the entire week, including weekends, may help limit these disruptions and support healthier circadian rhythms.

Industry observers note that "As someone who wakes up and goes to bed at the same time every day, I think a daily routine can be helpful for people of all ages across their lifespan," Tracy stated. "There is growing awareness about the concept of social jet lag -- waking up and going to bed at different times on weekends compared to weekdays -- and the disruptions it causes to our circadian rhythm, so hopefully this research helps more people consider the health benefits of a daily routine. Since one-third of our lives will be spent sleeping, I think health and well-being research should be looked at holistically from a 24-hour perspective and not just focus on when we are awake.".

A Simple Habit With Potential Health Benefits.

The research highlights an aspect of healthy living that can be easy to overlook. While getting enough quality sleep remains vital, the consistency of activities throughout the day may also be connected to how people feel physically and emotionally.

Recent findings suggest that because the study relied on survey data from a relatively small group of older adults, it cannot prove that adopting a regular routine will relieve pain or depression. Larger studies would be needed to establish whether changing daily schedules directly improves these outcomes.

Still, the findings suggest that a predictable daily routine may be a useful component of a broader approach to health, particularly for people experiencing insomnia.

For older adults and potentially people of other ages, simple habits such as maintaining regular waking times, eating meals on a consistent schedule, and limiting major changes in weekend sleep patterns may help support the body's natural rhythms.

The study, "Behavioral-social rhythms and insomnia symptoms: associations with pain, body mass index, and depressive symptoms among older adults," was published in the Journal of Behavioral Medicine.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • SpaceX rolled out a classified mission for the U.S.
  • A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:20 p.m.
  • The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth about 8.5 minutes later, touching down in the Pacific Ocean atop the SpaceX drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You." It was the 11th launch and landing for this booster, which is designated B1100.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX rolled out a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force tonight (Nov. 20), sending a mystery payload to orbit from California's central coast.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:20 p.m. EST (8:20 p.m. local California time; 0420 GMT on Nov. 21), on a Space Force mission called USSF-317.

The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth about 8.5 minutes later, touching down in the Pacific Ocean atop the SpaceX drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You." It was the 11th launch and landing for this booster, which is designated B1100.

SpaceX ended its launch webcast just after that touchdown, so we didn't get to see the Falcon 9's upper stage power its way to orbit.

Sources indicate that USSF-317 is a classified mission, so we don't know what the upper stage is carrying or where exactly it's headed. However, some experts think that USSF-317 may be hauling a batch of SpaceX's Starshield satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO) for the Space Force's Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, which helps the military keep tabs on potential targets around the world.

NROL-105 | USSF-385 | 8 Starlink missions.

USSF-317 was the 121st Falcon 9 launch of 2026 and the third mission that SpaceX has released for the Space Force so far in November.

The vast majority of this year's Falcon 9 missions — about 70% of them — have been devoted to building out SpaceX's Starlink LEO internet constellation, which presently consists of more than 11,000 satellites.

The Falcon 9 has been putting up incredible numbers lately — it flew a whopping 165 times in 2025, for example — but the workhorse rocket is on its way out. SpaceX prepares to retire both it and the Falcon Heavy in favor of its fully reusable Starship megarocket, which deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites on its most recent two test flights.

#93979. Industry News: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections

Industry News: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1821 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly important role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections.
  • It has been revealed that arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods.
  • Now, new research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly important role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections. Scientists at Rockefeller University have discovered that when the body runs low on arginine, a key part of its immune defense system can stop working properly, potentially allowing dangerous cells and viruses to escape detection.

It has been revealed that arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods. It is essential for making proteins that perform countless functions throughout the body. Researchers have long known that unusually low arginine levels are associated with several diseases, including colon cancer, but exactly how this shortage affects the body's defenses has remained unclear.

Now, new research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats. In experiments involving mice, increasing dietary arginine reduced the formation of colon cancer tumors and lessened the severity of influenza and SARS-CoV-2 infections. Remarkably, providing arginine after mice had already contracted influenza also improved their outcomes.

The findings, published in the journal Cell, raise the possibility that an inexpensive, readily available supplement could eventually become a useful addition to cancer treatments and strategies for combating viral infections. However, further research in humans is needed to determine whether the benefits observed in mice translate into effective treatments for people.

How a Missing Nutrient Could Help Cancer Escape the Immune System.

The research was led by Sohail Tavazoie, who directs the Elizabeth and Vincent Meyer Laboratory of Systems Cancer Biology at Rockefeller University. His team has spent years investigating how arginine influences cancer development and progression.

According to recent reports, in 2023, the researchers discovered that depriving colon cancer cells of arginine caused them to accumulate more genetic mutations. These changes can contribute to the unpredictable behavior of cancer cells, raising notable questions about how arginine shortages might influence the disease.

Industry observers note that the latest study reveals another potentially significant consequence. When arginine becomes scarce, cells struggle to produce enough of a crucial immune system protein known as MHC-1. This protein acts as a warning system, helping immune cells identify potential dangers such as cancerous changes or viral infections.

Without enough MHC-1, abnormal or infected cells may become harder for the immune system to recognize.

Encouragingly, the researchers also found that supplying a moderate amount of arginine, comparable to the quantity available in a couple of over-the-counter supplement tablets, could help restore production of this important protein.

"Our work reveals how a lack of arginine interferes with the immune system, and suggests that upping arginine intake could prove beneficial," claims first author Qiushuang Wu, a postdoc in the lab. "Perhaps that means it could be used in combination with other therapies to treat both cancer and viral infections.".

Industry observers note that "Arginine supplementation could be readily tested in patients receiving immunotherapies or given to high-risk populations exposed to viral pathogens," Tavazoie suggests. "Considering that arginine is inexpensive and readily available, we hope that therapeutic and preventative studies could be undertaken soon.".

The Surprising Connection Between Arginine and Immune Defenses.

To understand why arginine has such an key effect, the researchers investigated how cells use amino acids to manufacture proteins.

Proteins are built from amino acids according to genetic instructions encoded in DNA. These instructions are copied into messenger RNA, which carries the information to the cellular machinery responsible for protein production.

Industry observers note that the instructions are read in groups of three genetic letters called codons. Each codon specifies an amino acid or provides another signal needed during protein production. Arginine is unusual in that six different codons can specify it, reflecting the multiple ways its incorporation into proteins can be encoded.

Scientists already knew that changes in amino acid availability could affect cellular metabolism and signaling, two processes that help regulate how cells obtain energy and respond to their surroundings. What remained less clear was whether shortages of particular amino acids could directly influence which proteins cells produce.

In a recent development, to investigate, Wu examined the effects of arginine availability across several disease models, including colon cancer, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2. Each of these diseases has previously been associated with abnormal levels of various amino acids.

The research was supported in part by the Stavros Niarchos Foundation (SNF) Institute for Global Infectious Disease Research at The Rockefeller University and the Weill Cancer East Hub.

"One of the most dramatic patterns to emerge was that arginine was the most depleted amino acid in all of these diseases," she indicates.

Why Low Arginine Levels Can Disrupt the Immune System.

In laboratory experiments using cultured cells, Wu examined how arginine shortages affected protein production. She identified 414 proteins whose levels dropped abnormally when arginine was scarce.

It has been revealed that many of these proteins were associated with biological functions already known to depend on arginine. However, the researchers uncovered a more unexpected effect involving three genes from the HLA family.

These genes provide instructions for producing proteins associated with MHC-I (major histocompatibility complex class I), an essential component of the immune system's ability to recognize threats.

MHC-I proteins are displayed on the surfaces of cells throughout the body. They act somewhat like identification displays, presenting small fragments of proteins from inside the cell to immune cells known as T cells.

When these displays reveal suspicious material, such as proteins produced by a virus or abnormal proteins associated with cancer, T cells can recognize the danger and help coordinate an immune response.

But the researchers found that arginine deficiency interfered with the production of these molecular warning signals.

Recent findings suggest that the reason involved ribosomes, the tiny cellular machines that assemble proteins by following genetic instructions. Because the proteins involved in MHC-I production require arginine at numerous points, the researchers suspected that an insufficient supply could interfere with their assembly.

Sources indicate that further experiments confirmed that suspicion. When arginine was unavailable, ribosomes stalled while trying to manufacture MHC-I proteins. Without enough of the required amino acid, the cells could not efficiently complete the process.

In a recent development, as a result, fewer MHC-I proteins reached the cell surface, reducing the signals that would normally alert T cells to cancer-associated or viral proteins. This created an opportunity for dangerous cells to avoid immune detection.

Sources indicate that "These findings are exciting because they reveal that consumption of a specific amino acid can directly regulate gene expression in an organism by increasing production of a protein enriched in that amino acid," Tavazoie indicates. "We believe that such selective translational tuning of gene expression through dietary manipulation likely extends to many other proteins and amino acids.".

More Arginine Meant Fewer Colon Cancer Tumors in Mice.

After identifying the molecular mechanism, Wu investigated whether changing the amount of arginine in an animal's diet could influence disease outcomes.

Mice receiving diets low in arginine developed more colon cancer tumors. In contrast, mice consuming higher amounts of the amino acid developed fewer tumors.

These findings provided evidence that arginine availability can influence cancer development through its effects on the immune system, rather than simply changing how individual cancer cells behave.

The results also raised a broader question: If arginine helps immune cells recognize cancer, could it provide similar benefits when the body encounters dangerous viruses?

Arginine Also Improved Outcomes From Influenza and COVID-19 Viruses.

To explore that possibility, Wu collaborated with Heinz-Heinrich Hoffman, a research assistant professor in Charles Rice's Laboratory of Virology and Infectious Disease.

Together, they examined the effects of dietary arginine in mouse models of influenza and SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19.

The findings followed the same general pattern seen in the colon cancer experiments. Mice consuming more arginine experienced less severe symptoms from viral infections, suggesting that adequate levels of the amino acid helped support the body's immune defenses.

The researchers then made an even more surprising discovery.

Industry observers note that arginine did not appear to be beneficial only when consumed before an infection. Giving mice additional arginine after they had already been infected with influenza also improved their outcomes.

Recent findings suggest that "Not only did mice with an arginine-rich diet have milder symptoms from viral infections, giving the mice arginine after influenza infection improved their outcomes too," Wu notes. "That was very surprising. From our genetic models, we knew manipulating arginine levels had a strong effect on gene expression, but we didn't expect the dietary manipulation to be equally impactful.".

The observation suggests that changing nutrient availability might influence how the immune system responds even after a viral infection has taken hold.

Could a Simple Supplement Improve Cancer and Virus Treatments?

The discovery has potentially vital implications for understanding why some people become more vulnerable to cancer and severe viral infections.

Sources indicate that arginine levels naturally decline with age, and inadequate nutrition can further reduce the amount available to cells. The researchers suspect that these changes may contribute to the weakening of immune defenses seen in certain diseases and in older adults.

"Qiushuang's findings illuminate how poor diet and aging -- during which arginine levels naturally decline -- could create the perfect storm for the initiation of colon cancer. Similarly, age-related arginine loss could partially contribute to the greater mortality caused by respiratory viruses," Tavazoie claims. "We're also investigating whether making dietary changes in other amino acids has beneficial effects in a variety of disease contexts. There are no doubt more discoveries to come.".

Industry observers note that the possibility of using arginine alongside existing cancer immunotherapies is particularly intriguing. These treatments work by helping the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. If low arginine levels interfere with the molecular signals required for that recognition, restoring the nutrient might help some treatments work more effectively.

The researchers also see potential for investigating arginine supplementation in people at elevated risk of respiratory viral infections.

For now, these possibilities remain experimental. The findings do not establish that taking arginine supplements prevents or treats cancer, influenza, or COVID-19 in humans.

Nevertheless, the research reveals an crucial connection between nutrition and immunity. Rather than simply providing the raw materials needed to build proteins, specific amino acids may help determine how effectively the body's immune defenses identify and respond to dangerous threats.

And because arginine is inexpensive and widely available, the discovery could provide a practical starting point for future studies aimed at strengthening the immune system against cancer and infectious diseases.

A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising latest study

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1493 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that an existing osteoporosis drug has shown surprising promise in protecting the spine from damage, raising hopes for latest treatments for chronic neck and back pain.
  • According to recent reports, the discovery could help scientists tackle one of the underlying causes of back pain: the gradual deterioration of the discs that cushion the bones of the spine.
  • In a recent development, although the findings have not yet been confirmed in humans, they suggest that medications already used for other conditions could offer latest ways to slow spinal degeneration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that an existing osteoporosis drug has shown surprising promise in protecting the spine from damage, raising hopes for latest treatments for chronic neck and back pain. In experiments involving zebrafish, researchers found that the medication prevented abnormal mineral deposits from forming in the spine, a process that can cause spinal tissues to harden and vertebrae to fuse together.

According to recent reports, the discovery could help scientists tackle one of the underlying causes of back pain: the gradual deterioration of the discs that cushion the bones of the spine. Researchers also identified changes in gene activity and metabolism that appear to contribute to this damage, revealing several possible targets for future treatments.

In a recent development, although the findings have not yet been confirmed in humans, they suggest that medications already used for other conditions could offer latest ways to slow spinal degeneration. The research also demonstrates how zebrafish could help scientists investigate the causes of spinal disease and test potential therapies.

Most people experience back pain at some point in their lives, and one common cause is the deterioration of the spine's natural shock absorbers. These structures, called intervertebral discs, sit between the vertebrae and help the spine absorb pressure, distribute weight, and move comfortably.

Over time, the discs can lose their ability to cushion the spine, a condition known as intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD). As the discs deteriorate, they can contribute to pain, stiffness, and reduced mobility.

Sources indicate that despite the widespread impact and substantial economic burden of this condition, no medications are currently available that can stop or reverse the degenerative process. Surgery remains the only established long-term intervention for certain severe cases, creating an urgent need for treatments that address the underlying damage.

Sources indicate that researchers have long known that genetics influences the risk of developing spinal disc degeneration. One gene of particular interest is associated with collagen IX, a protein that helps maintain the structural integrity of spinal discs by supporting the network of fibers that holds them together. Variations affecting this gene have repeatedly been associated with disc problems that develop earlier in life.

Industry observers note that to investigate how these genetic changes contribute to spinal damage, scientists at the Universities of Edinburgh and Bristol turned to zebrafish. They studied fish that had been bred without a functioning copy of the gene, allowing them to observe how its absence affected the spine as the animals grew older.

A Hidden Process Causes the Spine To Harden.

The results revealed striking similarities between the genetically altered zebrafish and people with degenerative spinal disease.

Recent findings suggest that as the fish aged, abnormal mineral deposits accumulated in the tissues separating their vertebrae. This process, known as mineralization, involves minerals collecting in tissues where they do not normally belong. In the spine, the buildup can cause normally flexible structures to become unusually rigid, much like unwanted bone forming in the wrong location.

In a recent development, the researchers also observed spinal fusion, in which neighboring vertebrae become joined together. Such changes can interfere with the spine's normal flexibility and movement.

Sources indicate that importantly, the scientists discovered that the damage began well before the mineral deposits appeared. An underlying layer that provides structural support during spinal development started to break down first, suggesting that deterioration of this protective framework may set the stage for later hardening.

This finding could help explain how genetic changes initiate a chain reaction that eventually damages the spine.

Surprising Links to Fat Metabolism and Vitamin A.

Sources indicate that to understand what was happening at the molecular level, the team examined patterns of gene activity in the zebrafish. This allowed them to identify biological processes that had become unusually active or disrupted as spinal degeneration developed.

Several unexpected connections emerged.

Industry observers note that the researchers found alterations in fat metabolism, the processes through which the body breaks down, stores, and uses fats. They also detected disturbances in a cellular signaling system called mTOR, which helps regulate cell growth, metabolism, and responses to nutrients.

Sources indicate that additional changes involved phosphate regulation and vitamin A signaling. Phosphate is an essential mineral involved in building bones and teeth, but its accumulation in the wrong tissues can contribute to abnormal hardening. Vitamin A signaling helps control how cells develop and function.

Recent findings suggest that together, these findings suggest that spinal disc degeneration involves more than the gradual wearing down of tissues. Changes in how cells process nutrients, regulate growth, and handle minerals may also play important roles.

An Osteoporosis Drug Blocks Spinal Mineral Buildup.

One of the most promising discoveries came when researchers tested ways to reduce the spinal abnormalities.

A medication belonging to a class of drugs called bisphosphonates successfully blocked the abnormal mineral buildup in the zebrafish. Bisphosphonates are already used to treat osteoporosis, a condition in which bones become weaker and more vulnerable to fractures. These medications help protect bones by slowing the processes that break down bone tissue.

The finding is especially intriguing because it suggests that a treatment already used in patients might also help researchers develop therapies for spinal degeneration.

The team identified other approaches that reduced spinal damage. Limiting how much food the zebrafish consumed led to fewer spinal fusions, as did medications that suppressed fat metabolism.

These results point toward fat metabolism and phosphate regulation as potentially notable targets for future drugs.

Industry observers note that however, the experiments were conducted in zebrafish, not humans. More research will be needed to determine whether the same biological mechanisms operate in people and whether targeting them can safely prevent or slow spinal disc degeneration. The dietary findings also do not establish that restricting food intake can prevent spinal damage in humans.

New Hope for Chronic Back Pain Treatments.

The study was published in the journal Communications Biology and received support from Arthritis UK and BBSRC.

Dr. Erika Kague, who led the research at the University of Edinburgh's Institute of Genetics and Cancer, emphasized the potential significance of identifying treatments that target the underlying causes of spinal damage.

In a recent development, "For decades, surgery has been the only real answer for disc disease. By understanding the biology that drives the spine to harden, our zebrafish studies point to several ways of slowing it down, including a drug already used safely in patients. There's more work to do, but for a condition that's affected people for generations without a treatment in sight, this is super exciting.".

The findings could be particularly crucial for the millions of people who live with persistent back pain and have limited options for preventing their condition from worsening.

It has been revealed that dr. Caroline Aylott, Head of Research Delivery at Arthritis UK, highlighted the potential benefits for patients.

"For the 9.5 million people across the UK living with back pain this research brings fresh hope that potential new therapeutic approaches are on the horizon.

In a recent development, "We are proud to fund research that is unlocking the science behind the processes leading to spinal disc degeneration. Back pain is one of the UK's most common conditions that has blighted millions over generations. Dr. Erika Kague and her team at the University of Edinburgh have uncovered notable genetic evidence that could pave the way for newly introduced treatments, bringing us one step closer to a future where fewer people have to live with the daily pain and challenges that back pain can bring.".

The research also illustrates the broader value of studying basic biological processes to understand diseases that affect large numbers of people.

Dr. Jef Grainger, Executive Director for Bioscience Advancing Knowledge at BBSRC, said:.

"This research reveals how publicly funded discovery bioscience can generate the knowledge needed to address major health challenges. By revealing new knowledge of how healthy biological processes break down in aging-related spinal disc degeneration, the study opens up promising avenues for future treatment development. It's a great example of how BBSRC-supported research helps turn scientific discovery into knowledge and innovations that have the potential to improve people's lives.".

By identifying genetic and metabolic changes that contribute to spinal hardening, and demonstrating that some of the damage can be prevented in zebrafish, the researchers have opened several new avenues for investigating spinal disc degeneration.

For a condition that affects millions and has no approved drug capable of stopping its progression, these early findings offer an encouraging starting point for developing treatments that could one day protect the spine before serious damage occurs.

  • Janelt scores stunner as Brentford beat 10-man Everton.

  • Prior to Monday night, the defender had received 74 yellow cards in the Premier League but had never been sent off - a top-flight record.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Janelt scores stunner as Brentford beat 10-man Everton.

It had been some run for Everton captain James Tarkowski.

Prior to Monday night, the defender had received 74 yellow cards in the Premier League but had never been sent off - a top-flight record.

But that run came to an end at Brentford as he was given his first red card in his 351st Premier League appearance, although the decision has attracted plenty of debate.

His dismissal crucially means he will miss Sunday's Merseyside derby and also ruined David Moyes' record-breaking night as he took charge of his 593rd game as Everton boss - more than anyone else in the club's history.

The 4-0 loss was also the heaviest defeat Everton have had since Moyes returned to the club at the start of last year.

Tarkowski's dismissal proved a big talking point during and after the match, with opinions split on whether he should have gone. Even Moyes wasn't sure.

According to recent reports, he told BBC Match of the Day: "My thoughts at the time, I didn't think it was but when I've looked at it again I think his foot high. Is there enough force for it to be a red card? Not sure about that.".

James Tarkowski received his first Premier League red card.

Just 15 minutes after Keane Lewis-Potter scored his second deflected strike of the evening, Everton skipper Tarkowski thundered into a challenge on Brentford's Yehor Yarmoliuk.

He won the ball but also followed through with the challenge forcefully. Initially, referee Craig Pawson deemed a foul and a yellow card was enough.

But, after an intervention from the video assistant referee (VAR) and studying the replay, Pawson changed the yellow for a red.

The Premier League match centre said on X: "After VAR review, the referee overturned the original decision of yellow card for Tarkowski for the challenge on Yarmoliuk and issued a red card for serious foul play.

"VAR: 'Point of contact is on the shin. He's got speed and intensity. Studs are high.'.

Recent findings suggest that "REF: 'After review, Everton No.6 commits a challenge that endangers his opponent's safety, making contact with the studs onto the shin. Cancelling the yellow card - and a red card.'".

Referees are asked to take into account several considerations for what counts as serious foul play including the speed of the challenge, its intensity, force and what degree of control there was.

But, as always, there was plenty of debate about whether it was the correct decision.

BBC Sport's football issues correspondent Dale Johnson, said: "Really not sure about this as a VAR red card.

"Yes, Tarkowski absolutely ticks the boxes for speed and intensity and leading high with studs showing.

"But the question marks are that Tarkowski made only small contact and didn't have a straight leg when he did so.

In a recent development, "Maybe his reputation played a part? Remember, he wrongly escaped a VAR red card against Liverpool for a challenge, which was along the same lines. He won the ball and then followed through into Alexis Mac Allister. Thought that was a far stronger challenge.".

BBC Radio 5 Live's - and former Blackburn Rovers striker - Chris Sutton, stated on X: "Come on that's not a redâ¦ the game's gone.".

In a recent development, former Arsenal striker Alan Smith agreed the decision was harsh. He told Sky Sports: "Ten years ago we wouldn't have looked at it once and now we still [frame] it on the follow-through. I just can't see it.

In a recent development, "Only Tarkowski knows if he wanted to leave it high or if it was natural. The follow-through was just natural momentum.

"There's a bit of anger in there from Tarkowski and it's a little high but only he knows if he wanted to leave a little more on Yarmoliuk there.".

Opinion was far from unanimous though, with both pundits in the Sky Sports studio adamant it was a clear red.

Former Liverpool centre-back Jamie Carragher remarked: "It's a red card. Tarkowski has got previous for tackles like that. He is a 90s defender, he tackles like that.

In a recent development, "He follows through with such force, it is excessive. You want to give him the benefit of the doubt but it's a red card.".

Recent findings suggest that he added: "You could argue was it a significant enough mistake for VAR to get involved but I think we are splitting hairs. He doesn't need to do this.".

While ex-Totenham defender Toby Alderweireld added: "It's a red card, he knows what he is doing. 100%.".

Brentford 4-0 Everton: David Moyes post-match interview.

Josh, Sheffield: Never a red for Tarkowski and I'm a Liverpool fan. What's he meant to do? Stop momentum. It's a good tackle and the player runs into the natural follow through.

Recent findings suggest that robin, Essex: Another game ruined by VAR! Not straight leg tackle you can surely see he turned his foot around. Poor!

In a recent development, lee: It is a sad day when a good tackle gets a player sent off. You slow anything down and dissect it you can find wrongs. Yellow was a bit much and the red ridiculous, we need ex players in the VAR decisions too.

Industry observers note that max, Oldham: What a load of nonsense the red card is. Tarkowski can't stop his momentum. VAR has ruined another game, plus what is the ref doing? He had a chance to stick with the yellow card. Another case of an official who has never played the game.

It has been revealed that paul, St Asaph: Tarkowski has got away with that same foul a few times. Do think he's the type of player to leave one in on purpose.

Anon: Yes it's a red - Tarkowski knows what he's doing, it's frustration and wanting to leave a bit on the player.

Chris, Chelmsford: He does it all the time at the borderline but about time he got one.

Woody, London: Lack of refinement masked as passion, classic Tarkowski tackle thereâ¦ glad to see him off.

George, Birmingham: Studs up in a tackle, he has to go. A clear red card for me.

Home Depot on Tuesday declared its chief financial officer, Richard McPhail, will become CEO of the company, succeeding Ted Decker, effective next week.

It has been revealed that alongside McPhail's appointment, Home Depot said Ann-Marie Campbell, currently senior executive vice president of U.S. stores and operations, will become president and chief operating officer. Jordan Broggi has been chosen as CFO to succeed McPhail.

Decker, CEO since 2022, had been on temporary medical leave since August. The tech giant said on Tuesday that Decker has returned from leave but is now stepping down from his role. He will continue to serve as chair of the board of directors, the company said.

It has been revealed that "I'm glad to be back and grateful for the support I received," Decker told analysts on Tuesday. "The board and I have agreed that now is the right time to move to the next phase of our succession initiative.".

McPhail has been with the tech giant since 2005, holding multiple executive roles.

"We're not going to change course," McPhail told CNBC's Becky Quick.

In a recent development, he stated the company will continue to lean into winning professional shoppers like contractors and using artificial intelligence tools to encourage sales. McPhail added that while the company faces more challenges now than it did at the start of the year, it is still winning share of the home improvement market.

In a recent development, home Depot has been pressured by a sluggish housing market, higher mortgage rates and a more cautious consumer. Still, the organization has previously noted it's seen resilience among its pro shoppers who are still shopping for their home improvement projects.

Shares of Home Depot sank more than 3% following the announcement and the retailer's fiscal third-quarter results.

The CEO change came as the home improvement retailer posted quarterly earnings and revenue that beat analysts' expectations. The manufacturer said comparable sales rose 2.2% during the period, compared with estimates of up 1.8%, according to StreetAccount.

Here's how Home Depot performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

Sources indicate that the firm reported net income of $3.71 billion, or $3.72 per share, compared with $3.60 billion, or $3.62 per share, the year prior. Excluding one-time items, Home Depot reported adjusted earnings per share of $3.86.

Revenue rose 4.9% compared with the year-ago period.

"We also are confident that we are taking material share from the market and from competition," McPhail noted on the call with analysts.

In the third quarter, the company said online comparable sales grew around 13%, which marked its sixth straight quarter of double-digit positive growth for the metric.

The manufacturer remarked it saw positive comparable sales numbers in 13 out of 16 of its merchandising departments, including notable strength in the power department, which posted double-digit percentage growth.

Recent findings suggest that for the full year, Home Depot said it expects total sales to rise roughly 4.5%, the top end of its previously provided range. It also anticipates comparable sales will grow around 1.4%, compared with an outlook of flat to a 2% increase.

Home Depot added it expects adjusted earnings per share to rise 2% this year, compared with prior guidance of flat to a 4% increase.

Industry observers note that boris Rosenfeld demonstrates DW a photo of him with his daughter Sofia and can't hold back tears. "This was the last time we saw her. Then she left for Moscow, and this whole case began," he states.

Helives in Israel, while Sofia is in Russia. For more than a month now, she has been behind bars on charges of financing extremism. The case goes back to two donations totaling 2,000 rubles (about $30) to the late opposition politician Alexei Navalny'sAnti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), which the Russian authorities have since designated as extremist.

On October 7, a court in Moscow sentenced Rosenfeld to three and a half years in a penal colony.

Recent findings suggest that rosenfeld is a prominent ornithologist who has devoted her life to studying and protecting Arcticbirds. "Sofia was an avid young naturalist from childhood. She loved birds, horses and dogs," her father stated as he leafed through a photo album.

Sofia was a teenager when the family moved to Israel but she returned to Russia a few years later and now holds both Russian and Israeli citizenship.

Recent findings suggest that she studied biology at Moscow State University and developed a significant scientific career in Russia. Her colleague, Alexandra Panyutina, who now also lives in Israel, explained that Rosenfeld was devoted to her work from an early age.

"Birds and the Arctic are the defining passions of her life," she said.

Rosenfeld was among the first Russian researchers to develop a systematic approach to monitoring migratory bird populations. To support her research, she even developed a special aircraft.

"They could fly at almost the same speed as the birds and observe them from a low altitude," claims Dmitry (name changed), a colleague of Rosenfeld's. "It rapidly became clear that this was a unique method.".

Rosenfeld is considered to be one of the leading figures in Russian ornithology. Her work has extended well beyond Russia and she has been deeply involved in international research projects. In the field of migratory bird conservation, cross-border cooperation is essential.

Helmut Kruckenberg, the head of the German Institute for Wetlands and Waterbird Research (IWWR), noted Rosenfeld was highly respected within the international scientific community.

"She has done an enormous amount for nature conservation and for the protection of Siberian and Arctic species," he remarked. "What is happening to her is simply beyond comprehension for us.".

According to recent reports, in the summer of 2021, when Russian authorities designated Alexei Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation, also known as FBK, as an extremist organization, Rosenfeld was on a remote Arctic expedition without a phone or access to the internet. Therefore, she did not cancel her regular donations to the FBK immediately, doing so only after her return to the Russian capital Moscow.

Recent findings suggest that her friend Olga (name changed) described Sofia as a person of absolute honesty. According to her, Rosenfeld's donations to Navalny's foundation reflected a genuine desire to fight corruption. Through her work in Russia's regions, she had seen plenty of it firsthand.

"She was never involved in political activism. Her donations were solely intended to support anti-corruption work," stated her father Boris Rosenfeld. "It's unthinkable".

Industry observers note that for him and others close to her, the sentence came as a shock. Although prosecutors had requested a five-year prison term, friends and colleagues expected that she would receive a fine at most.

Recent findings suggest that there were reasons for that expectation. According to calculations by independent media outlet Mediazona, about 85% of convictions in the 225 cases involving donations to Navalny's foundation have so far resulted in non-custodial sentences. Yet Rosenfeld got three and a half years in a penal colony.

Recent findings suggest that just a few months after Rosenfeld defended her doctoral dissertation in October 2025, her home was searched. She was also subject to travel restrictions. She continued to work but she had to cancel her annual summer expedition to the Arctic.

Even on the day of the sentencing, her conversations with  her colleagues focused largely on science:  "We discussed how the work could continue in Sofia's absence," Olga noted. "But no one really believed she would end up in prison.".

"The only thing we think about now is how to bring her here," Boris Rosenfeld says as he looks at the pictures from Sofia's last visit.

Friends and colleagues who spoke to DW say that his daughter never considered leaving Russia, even as the prospect of a prison sentence loomed. "Sofia would never have left. She simply can't imagine life without geese," indicates Dmitry.

Sources indicate that now, her family, friends and colleagues are campaigning to have her sentence overturned. More than 1,000 people have signed an appeal to Russia's Presidential Council for Human Rights.

Boris Rosenfeld is also hoping for support from Israel but so far Israeli consular officials have not been granted access to his daughter in detention.

The two continue to write to each other and he is trying to keep his spirits high: "She writes that she's trying to adjust to life in prison, and that it's hard," he says. "But she's a strong person.".
